Latest Update: Common forever chemicals linked to nearly double the rate of aggressive breast cancer

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that women with higher blood levels of two common "forever chemicals" may face an increased risk of developing a particularly aggressive form of breast cancer, according to new research from the National Institutes of Health (NIH), part of the U.S.
  • The study identified a connection between estrogen receptor-negative, or ER-negative, breast cancer and two widely encountered chemicals: perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS).
  • Both substances belong to a large family of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, commonly called PFAS.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that women with higher blood levels of two common "forever chemicals" may face an increased risk of developing a particularly aggressive form of breast cancer, according to new research from the National Institutes of Health (NIH), part of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).

The study identified a connection between estrogen receptor-negative, or ER-negative, breast cancer and two widely encountered chemicals: perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS). Women with greater concentrations of these substances in their blood were more likely to develop this type of cancer. However, researchers found no clear link between either chemical and breast cancer risk overall.

Both substances belong to a large family of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, commonly called PFAS. These chemicals have been used in numerous everyday consumer products and are often described as "forever chemicals" because they resist breaking down in the environment. They can also accumulate in the human body and remain there for years.

"Women deserve clear answers about how chemicals in their environment may affect their health," mentioned HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. "This NIH study links two forever chemicals to a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer and demands further investigation. Under President Trump's leadership, we will pursue the evidence, confront environmental health risks, and give women the information they need to protect their health.".

Why This Aggressive Breast Cancer Is Concerning.

Sources indicate that ER-negative breast cancer differs from more common forms of the disease because its tumor cells lack the receptors that allow estrogen to stimulate cancer growth. These cancers are often more aggressive and generally have poorer outcomes than tumors that respond to estrogen.

It has been revealed that despite their severity, researchers still have relatively little information about what makes someone more likely to develop ER-negative breast cancer. The new findings suggest that exposure to certain persistent environmental chemicals could be one contributing factor.

"Our findings, which we confirmed using a meta-analysis of prior research, indicate that certain legacy PFAS, including PFOA and PFOS, are associated with a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer, a more aggressive tumor type with few known risk factors," explained NIH Stadtman Investigator Alexandra White, Ph.D., who led the study.

The findings were published in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.

Higher Forever Chemical Levels Linked to Greater Cancer Risk.

It has been revealed that to investigate the possible connection, NIH scientists and their collaborators examined blood samples that had been collected years before participants received a cancer diagnosis. The researchers measured concentrations of 17 different PFAS chemicals, allowing them to compare earlier exposure levels with subsequent breast cancer outcomes.

In a recent development, the results revealed substantial differences for two chemicals. Women in the highest PFOA exposure group had a 67% higher rate of ER-negative breast cancer than women in the lowest group. The association was even stronger for PFOS, with the highest exposure group showing a 93% higher rate, nearly twice that of the lowest group.

In a recent development, these percentages represent relative differences between groups rather than the absolute probability that an individual woman will develop breast cancer. The findings also establish an association, not proof that the chemicals directly cause the disease.

Industry observers note that the analysis used data from the Sister Study, a major research project conducted by NIH's National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS). Between 2003 and 2009, the study enrolled 50,884 women ages 35-74 from across the United States and Puerto Rico.

All participants were free of breast cancer when they enrolled, although each had a full or half-sister who had already been diagnosed with the disease. For the PFAS investigation, researchers analyzed information from 1,609 women who subsequently developed breast cancer and a comparison group of 2,269 women.

Could Reducing PFAS Exposure Lower Cancer Risk?

It has been revealed that although PFAS can remain in the environment and the body for long periods, researchers emphasize that exposure is not necessarily unavoidable. The findings could eventually help identify new ways to reduce the risk of aggressive breast cancer.

"These findings matter for women's health broadly," mentioned first author, Che-Jung Chang, Ph.D., who previously worked as an NIH research fellow and is now a researcher at DLH, a scientific research organization. "Although PFAS are persistent in the environment and in our bodies, exposure to them is still potentially modifiable, meaning people can take steps to reduce their exposure, and these findings could open new avenues for prevention.".

The researchers are also interested in understanding how these chemicals might influence cancer development. Because the strongest associations appeared in tumors that lack estrogen receptors, the findings suggest that PFAS could act through biological processes unrelated to hormonal signaling.

Recent findings suggest that potential explanations include changes in gene activity or alterations in the immune system. However, the study did not directly investigate these mechanisms, so their involvement remains uncertain.

Newer Forever Chemicals Raise Unanswered Questions.

It has been revealed that although PFOA and PFOS have largely been phased out and replaced with other PFAS compounds, measurable amounts of both substances are still present in most people's bodies. Their persistence means that exposure to these older chemicals remains a potential public health concern.

It has been revealed that the researchers say additional investigations should focus on populations with greater PFAS exposure, as well as groups that experience higher rates of ER-negative breast cancer. Such research could help clarify the strength of the observed associations and identify whether certain populations face greater risks.

Scientists also need to determine whether the newer chemicals introduced as replacements for PFOA and PFOS carry similar health concerns.

"More research is needed, particularly evaluating the risk of breast cancer associated with newer replacement PFAS chemicals," White said.

The findings add to growing questions about the long-term health effects of forever chemicals and highlight the importance of understanding how environmental exposures may contribute to aggressive forms of breast cancer.

The research received support from NIEHS grants Z01ES044005; Z1AES103332; and R01ES032831.

Materials provided by NIH/Office of the Director. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

HLTH 2026: Elsevier upgrades ClinicalKey AI with full patient EHR context

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1864 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fiercehealthcare

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
HLTH 2026: Elsevier upgrades ClinicalKey AI with full patient EHR context" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Elsevier unveiled this week a major upgrade to ClinicalKey AI, enabling the AI-powered clinical decision support tool to access a patient’s full electronic health record and evaluate treatment plans against the company’s evidence-based medical library.

As AI advances, Elsevier has strategically shifted from a traditional academic publisher—it’s one of the world's largest publishers of scientific, technical and medical content—to an AI-driven analytics information company, incorporating generative and agentic AI into its healthcare and academic research.

ClinicalKey AI is a HIPAA-ready point-of-care decision support tool that draws answers from articles sourced from approximately 1,000 world-leading journals. Elsevier’s upgraded ClinicalKey AI is already deployed at more than 1,200 hospitals, and the firm says the solution integrates with all EHR providers. Elsevier recently struck a content agreement with the JAMA Network that brings full-text content and visuals from the JAMA Network Family of Journals to ClinicalKey AI.

ClinicalKey AI was originally co-developed through a strategic partnership between Elsevier and OpenEvidence. An Elsevier spokesperson said the manufacturer's collaboration with OpenEvidence on ClinicalKey AI has concluded.

Industry observers note that the manufacturer has rapidly expanded its AI capabilities and features, including ClinicalKey Nursing AI, an AI-powered tool built specifically for nurses and nursing workflows. Elsevier has also developed specialized AI assistants, such as LeapSpace, an AI-assisted workspace for researchers that’s built on 15+ million peer-reviewed articles and book content and 100 million Scopus records, according to the company.

Sources indicate that three months ago, the tech giant rolled out its "Ask AI" feature across more than 1,500 U.S. hospital sites using its flagship ClinicalKey platform. With the generative AI feature, clinicians can ask conversational clinical questions and receive direct, cited answers drawn from evidence-based sources, including premium journals and content from leading medical organizations, the company remarked. Unlike general-purpose chatbots, Ask AI does not pull from the open web and does not store, process or retain patient-identifiable information, according to the company.

In a move to develop context-aware AI, the manufacturer acquired Wellsheet in June. The health technology company aggregates and synthesizes patient chart data—including notes, labs, imaging and medication orders—from EHRs to provide relevant clinical intelligence at the bedside.

“The problem we’re trying to solve here is that physicians are challenged by so many things when they’re taking care of patients; top among them is patient complexity. Patients have more and more conditions, and they’re taking more and more medications. It can be hard to really understand the full picture and determine how to proceed,” Dr. Claudine Lott, physician executive for clinical solutions at Elsevier, told Fierce Healthcare during the HLTH conference this week.

According to recent reports, “Our original ClinicalKey AI tool has been a place where the clinician can go, and they can ask a question, and it searches this curated database of evidence-based content we’ve given it and gives them an answer. But there was a bit of a missing piece in that it wasn’t capturing that patient context. If you wanted to get an answer, that’s really tailored to a patient, it was limited to what you can type in,” she said.

She added, “Wellsheet has 10 years of experience with looking at the entirety of the patient chart and helping to surface that to the clinician.”.

There is a growing market for AI-powered clinical decision support products, but Elsevier contends its advantage lies in its depth of patient context and its large, curated content base, with a wholly owned, large proprietary library of peer-reviewed STM literature, including content from millions of articles, journals and books.

San Juan Regional Medical Center in Farmington, New Mexico, is using ClinicalKey AI’s new patient context functionality to provide quality care with fewer resources. With smaller clinical and quality teams than large academic health systems, and in a state where nearly 40% of residents rely on Medicaid, the medical center, which serves the Four Corners area, has found this support especially valuable, according to Carlo Hallak, M.D., physician executive, information services, at San Juan Regional Medical Center.

A non-profit, community-owned acute care hospital and Level III trauma center, San Juan Regional Medical Center operates outpatient and specialty clinics alongside its main hospital campus, San Juan Regional Rehabilitation Hospital and San Juan Health Partners clinics.

In a recent development, hallak emphasized that Elsevier is a primary source of medical knowledge rather than a “wrapper” for other AI platforms, and that was a key distinction for the organization, he stated. And ClinicalKey AI is designed for the entire care team. “The hospital is run by nurses, mid-level providers, other caregiver teams,” he told Fierce Healthcare at the HLTH conference.

The medical center aims to move clinicians to enterprise LLMs integrated with the electronic health record that can provide the full patient context, Hallak said.

In a recent development, "We're already seeing how ClinicalKey AI can be instrumental at the bedside and help improve care for our patients. As a rural healthcare center, we are proud to say that by using ClinicalKey AI to check each patient’s care against the same evidence base that major health systems rely on, we’re able to deliver the standard of care patients expect in any major city or leading academic center," Hallak mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that he added, "ClinicalKey AI reads the whole chart, checks it against the evidence and shows exactly where each finding comes from. That support is invaluable for a hospital like ours, and we’re already seeing strong adoption of ClinicalKey AI among our clinicians.".

Hallak cited an example of a physician who used ClinicalKey AI to correctly identify viral meningitis, preventing an aggressive and unnecessary treatment course for bacterial meningitis.

Sources indicate that clinicalKey AI supports the physician’s judgment rather than replacing it, helping the clinician get to relevant evidence faster, he remarked, noting that, in the case of the viral meningitis patient, the physician’s clinical judgment was critical in recognizing that something was unusual and then consulting colleagues. The AI tool then helped accelerate the next step by quickly surfacing information the clinician otherwise would have found by searching the medical literature.

Physicians also use the tool during weekly complex case discussions to promptly review trending medications, images and test results in one summarized sheet, he noted.

“It’s going to expedite a lot of the work they do when it comes to these complex cases,” he said.

The AI solution can swiftly summarize a complex patient history at the point of care, and this can help care teams in the emergency department understand a frequent ED patient, Hallak noted.

According to recent reports, one patient has visited their emergency department 95 times in less than a year, in addition to making numerous visits to neighboring health systems, Hallak stated. When that patient arrives, clinicians who aren't familiar with him would traditionally have to dig through the chart to understand his history. With Elsevier's ClinicalKey AI tool, they can ask for a summary of the patient's recent visits and care and get that information within seconds, he noted.

Because patients who frequently visit hospital EDs typically receive care at multiple organizations, San Juan Regional Medical Center is also working with other local health systems on interoperability efforts so clinicians can get a more complete picture of what happened during the patient's visits across different facilities.

As a rural hospital with staffing constraints, technology is essential to filling workforce gaps and supporting care delivery, Hallak contends.

In a recent development, "We don't have enough physicians, enough nurses, enough transporters, enough caregivers. We will never be able to have enough of those," he mentioned.

Hallak envisions ClinicalKey AI will be particularly valuable for discharging patients from the hospital faster.

Generative AI tools can help speed up patient discharges by identifying barriers, assessing patients’ care needs and providing relevant information from both structured and unstructured data. Because the platform is designed for the broader care team, case managers and physicians can access the same information, while push notifications can alert clinicians when test results are available so they can act quickly, Hallak stated.

"From an operational perspective, it allows for this care team coordination of care, and also from a physician perspective, it provides the context whenever there's something hanging and they're trying to understand more what's happening with the patient['s] discharge. You could be a hospitalist, and you've been off shift for like seven days, and then you come to the hospital and now the patient is on their tenth day, but you inherit that discharge. Going through, reading every progress note for every single day, reading every consult for every subspecialty that looked at this patient usually would take two to three days to actually get the patient out of the building safely," he said.

Rather than manually compiling information for a discharge summary, clinicians can use ClinicalKey AI to aggregate relevant information from across the patient’s record, trace it back to its source and review the AI-generated summary before signing off on the discharge, according to Hallak.

"It is a game changer, in my opinion. One of our hospitals said it used to take me three days to discharge a patient; now it takes me less than three hours," he said.

Going forward, the system expects to measure operational outcomes such as length of stay, safe discharge and multidisciplinary-rounds use, according to Hallak. The medical center also plans to evaluate clinicians' use of the tool and how it changes care decisions.

The medical center has also deployed other AI tools such as Oracle Health's clinical AI agent for ambient documentation.

Sources indicate that "These things are crucial. We're hoping to bring in a clinical AI agent for nurses as well to help the whole care team be able to eliminate the noise, the friction that typically EHRs or IT would bring to the conversation," Hallak mentioned.

In a recent development, the medical center is taking a risk-based approach to AI governance, using source verification and peer review for AI-generated summaries while applying greater scrutiny to tools that are predictive or suggestive, Hallak noted. That oversight involves clinical experts as well as compliance, legal and cybersecurity teams along with traditional vendor security and product-vetting requirements.

AI governance should become stricter as the technology moves from summarizing information to recommending or taking actions, he said.

According to recent reports, elsevier designed ClinicalKey AI with security and trust in mind, including HIPAA compliance, citations that show where information comes from and safeguards that keep the tool from prescribing what clinicians should do. Instead, it surfaces relevant information to help clinicians make their own decisions, Lott remarked.

It has been revealed that "Health systems tell us two things stand in the way of adopting AI: tools that don’t work with their existing EHR partners, and concerns about security, compliance and responsible use," Omry Bigger, president of Clinical Solutions at Elsevier, mentioned. "ClinicalKey AI was designed to address both. As an EHR-supported and HIPAA-compliant ready solution, ClinicalKey AI integrates seamlessly across health systems to provide clinicians with trusted evidence and patient context that gives them tailored clinical insights for each patient at the point of care.".

Intuit sells Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68B, less than a third of what it paid

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (868 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that financial software firm Intuit Inc.
  • Coming five years after Intuit agreed to acquire Mailchimp for $12 billion, the sale price is less than a third of what the company paid.
  • Although Bending Spoons describes the transaction as all-cash, Intuit will reinvest $368 million of its proceeds in newly issued Bending Spoons shares.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 17:17 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Industry observers note that financial software firm Intuit Inc. today announced that it has agreed to sell its Mailchimp email marketing business to Italian technology holding company Bending Spoons S.p.A. for about $3.68 billion.

Coming five years after Intuit agreed to acquire Mailchimp for $12 billion, the sale price is less than a third of what the company paid. The 2021 purchase was the largest in Intuit’s history at the time.

Although Bending Spoons describes the transaction as all-cash, Intuit will reinvest $368 million of its proceeds in newly issued Bending Spoons shares. That leaves Intuit with $3.31 billion in cash from the sale, according to the companies. Included in the deal is The Rocket Science Group LLC, the legal entity behind Mailchimp. Closing is expected in early 2027, subject to regulatory approvals.

Selling Mailchimp is noted to sharpen Intuit’s focus on the artificial intelligence-native tools it has built to help businesses win fresh customers, manage their pipeline and grow. Once the deal closes, Intuit intends to use the cash proceeds to buy back its own shares before the end of fiscal 2027.

Jack Tam, a senior vice president at Intuit, noted the company is confident Bending Spoons “will lead Mailchimp to continued success in this next chapter.”.

Industry observers note that growth at Mailchimp has stalled in recent quarters. Revenue from the business fell 1% to $313 million in the quarter ended Oct. 31. Intuit’s full-year guidance has Mailchimp revenue coming in flat to down 1%. In November 2024, Chief Financial Officer Sandeep Aujla told analysts that Intuit was seeing higher churn from smaller Mailchimp customers.

It has been revealed that “Mailchimp is a powerful brand, built over two decades of reshaping the email marketing category and redefining how companies grow their audiences,” stated Luca Ferrari, co-founder and chief executive of Bending Spoons. “We’re honored to welcome it to Bending Spoons and excited about what we can accomplish together.”.

Ferrari added that Bending Spoons looks to invest substantially in Mailchimp after closing. According to Bending Spoons, the transformation of a business it acquires is typically deep, entailing reorganized teams, overhauled technology and redesigned user interfaces.

Founded in 2013, Bending Spoons has built a portfolio of digital businesses that includes AOL, Brightcove, Eventbrite, Evernote, Tractive, Vimeo and WeTransfer. Since listing on the Nasdaq in July, the tech giant has also completed acquisitions of Airtable Inc. for $1.285 billion and whiteboard platform Miro for $1.355 billion.

In a recent development, intuit announced the sale alongside its fiscal 2027 first-quarter results. For the quarter, it reported adjusted earnings per share of $2.91, up 56% from $1.87 in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $4.35 billion, up 12% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting adjusted earnings of $2.70 per share on revenue of $4.31 billion.

Sources indicate that for its fiscal second quarter, Intuit expects adjusted earnings per share of $3.17 to $3.22 on revenue of $4.93 billion to $4.95 billion. Intuit lowered its full-year revenue guidance to between $23.08 billion and $23.37 billion.

Behind the cut is Credit Karma, the company’s personal finance and credit score service, which is now forecast to grow 3% to 7% this fiscal year, down from 11% to 13% previously. Intuit reiterated its full-year adjusted earnings guidance of $22.88 to $23.12 per share. None of the guidance includes the effect of the Mailchimp sale.

Intuit shares fell more than 10% in after-hours trading.

Industry News: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vaccines may do more than protect people from the immediate effects of a viral infection.
  • Recent findings suggest that scientists at Pompeu Fabra University discovered that mice recovering from an acute viral infection experienced prolonged problems with their immune defenses.
  • Most people think of common viral infections, such as colds or stomach viruses, as temporary illnesses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vaccines may do more than protect people from the immediate effects of a viral infection. Fresh research suggests they could also help prevent lasting damage to the immune system that remains even after the virus has disappeared.

Recent findings suggest that scientists at Pompeu Fabra University discovered that mice recovering from an acute viral infection experienced prolonged problems with their immune defenses. Although the animals had successfully fought off the virus, their immune systems remained impaired, making it harder to respond to new threats. Remarkably, mice vaccinated before infection did not develop these problems, suggesting that vaccination may provide an additional layer of protection beyond preventing illness.

Most people think of common viral infections, such as colds or stomach viruses, as temporary illnesses. A virus enters the body, multiplies, causes symptoms, and is eventually brought under control by the immune system. Once symptoms disappear, recovery is generally considered complete. The immune response also creates protection against future encounters with the same virus.

But what if the immune system continues to experience harmful effects long after the infection appears to be over?

Viral Infections Can Leave Lasting Immune Damage.

Researchers from Pompeu Fabra University's Infection Biology Laboratory investigated this possibility in a study published in Cell Death & Disease.

According to recent reports, using mice with acute viral infections, the team examined what happened to their immune systems after the animals had recovered. They found that eliminating the virus did not necessarily restore normal immune function. Instead, the infection left behind changes that persisted well beyond the initial illness.

According to Andreas Meyerhans, an ICREA research professor at UPF, who led the research, "there is a general perception that an acute viral infection is a relatively minor and transient event: once the virus is controlled and the symptoms have resolved, the body has fully recovered and is back to normal. But this view may underestimate consequences that are not immediately visible and can persist long after the infection itself has resolved.".

The researchers traced these lingering effects to significant changes in the spleen, an organ that plays an key role in coordinating immune defenses. As the immune system fought to eliminate the virus, the spleen developed fibrosis, a condition involving the buildup of scar-like tissue. The arrangement and positioning of immune cells within the organ also became disrupted.

These structural changes interfered with the interactions between immune cells that are necessary to activate T cells. These specialized cells are essential to adaptive immunity because they help recognize and destroy infected cells.

As a result, the mice remained less capable of launching effective immune responses when exposed to upcoming challenges. Even though the original infection had been brought under control, their immune defenses continued to function poorly.

Industry observers note that "The infection can be controlled, but that does not necessarily mean that the host has fully recovered," says Dr. Paula Cebollada Rica, first author of the study. "Our findings show that the immune-related consequences of an acute viral infection can persist beyond the period in which the virus is detectable, leaving the animals in an immunocompromised state.".

Vaccination Prevented Lasting Immune System Damage.

Recent findings suggest that after identifying these long-term effects, the scientists investigated whether they could be avoided. They focused on vaccination, which prepares the immune system to recognize and fight a pathogen before an infection occurs.

Industry observers note that the results revealed a striking difference between vaccinated and unvaccinated animals. Mice that received vaccination before infection did not develop the spleen damage or immune dysfunction seen in the other group.

Their spleens maintained their normal structure, and their T cells continued to function at levels comparable to those of mice that had never been infected.

This finding suggests that vaccination can protect the immune system itself from some of the harmful consequences of fighting a viral infection. In the mouse model, vaccination not only protected against the disease caused by the virus but also preserved the animals' ability to respond to future immune challenges.

"Vaccinated animals did not experience T-cell dysfunction or splenic alterations after recovering from an acute viral infection. This means that vaccination not only prevented the disease resulting from the acute infection but also preserved the immune system's ability to cope with fresh challenges," Cebollada Rica explains.

A Hidden Benefit of Vaccines With Public Health Implications.

The findings broaden the potential benefits of vaccination by highlighting a form of protection that may not be immediately apparent. Beyond reducing the immediate effects of an infection, vaccines may also help prevent persistent changes that weaken immune defenses.

Although these results were obtained in mice and do not establish that the same effects occur in humans, they raise vital questions about how viral infections influence long-term immune health and how vaccination might help protect it.

In a recent development, the research also comes at a time when vaccination policies and infectious disease prevention efforts are increasingly influenced by political decisions. The researchers emphasize the importance of scientific evidence in understanding the full consequences of infections, particularly when policy choices can undermine coordinated efforts to prevent infectious diseases.

Understanding the broader benefits of vaccination could therefore influence not only medical care but also how public health officials explain the value of vaccines to the public.

In a recent development, "The benefits of vaccination highlighted by this research are important not only for healthcare, but also for how we communicate the value of vaccination to the population at large," Meyerhans states. "It is important that people are aware of the broader protection that vaccination can provide and continue to trust in vaccines as one of the most effective tools to prevent diseases. Put simply, vaccines provide strong health benefits at a relatively low cost to society.".

Their HOA Approved Their Backyard Fences. Now They’re Being Told To Tear Them Down.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1133 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Almost six years ago, Laura Burns-Sierra hired Home Depot to install a fence around her property in the Cypress Mill community near Tampa, FL.
  • Now, another organization indicates the fence has to come down.
  • According to recent reports, "We couldn't do anything, any construction, any fences, nothing, without HOA approval," Burns-Sierra tells Realtor.com®.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Almost six years ago, Laura Burns-Sierra hired Home Depot to install a fence around her property in the Cypress Mill community near Tampa, FL. She submitted the plans to her homeowners association, received written approval and had the fence professionally installed.

Now, another organization indicates the fence has to come down.

According to recent reports, "We couldn't do anything, any construction, any fences, nothing, without HOA approval," Burns-Sierra tells Realtor.com®. "I followed the procedures to the T.".

Burns-Sierra is among a group of homeowners in the Sun City Center neighborhood caught in an unusual dispute between their HOA and the Cypress Mill Community Development District, or CDD. The latter states fences installed within drainage easements are interfering with its ability to maintain the community's stormwater infrastructure and now need to be removed.

The conflict has left residents facing hundreds or even thousands of dollars in unexpected expenses—and raises an important question for homeowners everywhere:.

Is an HOA's written approval enough to protect you when another governing body has authority over your property?

At the center of the dispute is a distinction many homeowners may not realize exists.

It has been revealed that an HOA generally oversees community standards, including architectural approvals, landscaping, and fence design. A CDD, meanwhile, is a special-purpose local government that can be responsible for infrastructure such as roads, drainage systems, and stormwater ponds.

In Cypress Mill, those responsibilities overlap on portions of homeowners' properties designated as drainage easements.

Jonathan Ellis, a Florida attorney experienced in HOA law—but is not involved in the dispute directly—tells Realtor.com that HOA approval doesn't necessarily authorize a homeowner to build within an easement.

"The HOA is telling you we don't have an objection to the fence," Ellis explains. "That doesn't mean now you can build the fence and don't worry about federal law, municipal law, or requirements of the CDD.".

In other words, the HOA may have properly approved the fences under its own rules without resolving whether they complied with the district's separate requirements.

Ellis claims the similar names of the HOA and CDD can add to the confusion, particularly for homeowners who aren't familiar with the distinction between the two organizations.

Burns-Sierra indicates the community's drainage ponds had been maintained for years without her fence becoming an concern.

She had her fence installed in May 2021, after receiving written approval from the HOA. About five years later, around Sept. 1, 2026, she and other residents received notice that the structure encroached on a drainage easement and would have to be removed by Sept. 18.

Burns-Sierra claims maintenance contractors eventually arrived outside her home prepared to remove her fence and sought $625 for the work.

She refused, saying she wanted time to investigate the district's authority and understand why a fence that had been approved years earlier was suddenly unacceptable.

"I am not going to pay you no money to tear down my fence," she recalls telling the workers.

Neighbor Victor Abreu faced a similar predicament, although his circumstances were different.

Abreu tells Realtor.com that he received written HOA approval to install a gate connecting his home to an existing fence belonging to his neighbor.

When the CDD subsequently demanded that the structures obstructing the drainage easement be removed or relocated, Victor complied.

On Oct. 19 he paid a contractor $1,000 to install a latest section of fencing closer to his house, losing part of a garden he estimates had cost approximately $1,500.

The latest arrangement also created a wider opening between neighboring properties, raising concerns about privacy, security, and access to the pond behind their homes.

Victor claims he believes communication broke down between the two organizations.

According to recent reports, "I would blame both of them," he says. "I would say 50-50.".

The Cypress Mill CDD maintains that the drainage easements are essential to the neighborhood's stormwater management system.

Sources indicate that in a written response to Realtor.com, district counsel Whitney A. Sousa noted the ponds and drainage areas are subject to environmental permits and oversight, including requirements administered by the Southwest Florida Water Management District.

The district has a legal responsibility to ensure contractors can inspect, maintain, and repair the system.

Mason Leon, the CDD’s on-site manager, tells Realtor.com that the fencing situation eventually made one pond inaccessible to the district's aquatic maintenance contractor through authorized access routes.

According to Sousa, the matter was brought before the CDD board on Aug. 13, 2026. A subsequent review identified 11 properties with fences or other structures encroaching on drainage easements.

The district determined that the encroachments must be removed to preserve access for maintenance equipment, vehicles, and contractors.

Importantly, Sousa acknowledged that better coordination between the HOA and CDD might have prevented the dispute.

"Ideally, these easements would have been identified during the HOA's review process, and the CDD would have been contacted before the fences were approved or installed," she wrote.

The district plans to work with the HOA to clarify approval requirements going forward.

For homeowners already affected, however, the district expects them to cover the costs of removing or relocating their fences.

In a recent development, sousa said residents requesting additional time have received extensions. The district does not believe those expenses should be spread across the neighborhood through CDD assessments.

Although residents are understandably frustrated, Ellis cautions against assuming the HOA is legally responsible simply because it approved their projects.

"Normally it's the unit owner that's responsible," he says, referring to securing all necessary permissions before construction.

Sources indicate that he explains that an HOA's approval generally addresses its own governing documents, including covenants, conditions, and restrictions. It doesn't eliminate the need to comply with separate drainage easements, building regulations, or other legal requirements.

Contractors may also have a role in identifying restrictions before beginning work.

Ellis notes that some communities permit fences within easements on the condition that homeowners remove them when access is needed.

The Cypress Mill CDD, however, has determined that all identified encroachments must be removed.

For homeowners like Burns-Sierra and Abreu, the distinction between an HOA's authority and the district's legal responsibilities has proved expensive.

The dispute offers a cautionary lesson for anyone purchasing a home or planning an outdoor renovation.

Ellis recommends determining which organizations have authority over a property before undertaking improvements.

"Homebuyers want to make sure when they're buying a home that they know of each of the entities that has a say over their property," he says.

Recent findings suggest that that means checking recorded plats, property surveys, and easement documents before installing fences, patios, pools, or other improvements. Homeowners should also determine whether approvals are required from an HOA, CDD, municipality, county, or utility provider.

And when multiple organizations are involved, written approval from one shouldn't be mistaken for permission from all of them.

Consumers believe AI will be key in making healthcare simpler: survey" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Americans want a healthcare experience that's simpler and easier to understand, and artificial intelligence may be the key to getting there, a new survey demonstrates.

The poll, conducted by the Harris Poll and commissioned by Elevance Health, found that 82% of American patients view at least some part of healthcare information as a "foreign language," and close to half (45%) stated they made a healthcare decision they later regretted due to a lack of understanding.

The survey was conducted among 2,0001 adults in mid-July, and 74% said they have encountered a key barrier, such as understanding their health insurance or a medical bill. And only a quarter (27%) said they completely understand their own health coverage.

That stated, most (79%) of those surveyed said they believe AI can help to improve the healthcare experience overall.

Ratnakar Lavu, chief digital information officer at Elevance Health, told Fierce in an email that because the tech has the ability to swiftly surface and parse key data about a member or health need, it can serve as a central piece of the puzzle in making a more personalized experience.

In a recent development, "AI-enabled tools give us the ability to create a unique member context," he said. "Because of this digital technology, we can now truly 'know the person' and proactively work with them to help them manage their healthcare needs.".

For example, 82% of those surveyed said they would like to receive answers about healthcare as rapidly as they can use an app to order a food delivery, and 83% would like to easily access recommendations that pull from their health coverage, individual health needs and financial situation.

Seventy-two percent stated they would trust AI for accuracy on at least one type of information, such as an explanation of benefits, cost estimates or details on medication.

In a recent development, however, while many Americans believe AI can play a leading role in driving a better health experience, just 20% said they right now use the tech regularly as a source of information. And while 72% said they trusted the tech to surface key health information, 33% said they would trust an AI platform to translate their insurance benefits, and 30% said they trust the tech to estimate care costs.

Just 13% mentioned they would trust AI to make diagnoses.

Lavu said that healthcare organizations looking to roll out fresh tools need to avoid simply embedding AI into programs for the sake of it, and be transparent about both the use case as well as the role of the human in the loop.

The study also found that women were less likely than men to trust AI, and younger generations were more likely to use it as a source of healthcare information than older groups.

It has been revealed that "We have to implement AI at the speed of trust, which means being thoughtful about where AI adds value, not just delivering technology for technology’s sake," he said. "Trust is also earned when AI-enabled programs truly make things easier for the consumer. ".

Recent findings suggest that for example, Elevance Health has deployed an AI-powered program to support utilization management reviews and help drive faster approvals where possible, though AI is not used to make claims denials. It is also leaning on AI for more proactive member engagement initiatives through its digital channels, identifying individuals that would benefit from extra support or who may face gaps in care.

Sources indicate that "We start by listening to members and identifying where healthcare is creating the most confusion or friction," Lavu noted. "From there, we determine the right solution, which may or may not involve AI. When AI is the right tool, it should fit naturally into familiar interactions and make it easier for members to get an answer or take the next step.".

Stopping statins after 70 may be safer than expected, but there's a catch

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The independent, preliminary research was presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, held November 6 through 9 in Chicago.
  • It has been revealed that an estimated 25% of American adults have elevated levels of low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C), commonly called "bad cholesterol." When too much LDL cholesterol accumulates in the arteries, it can restrict blood flow and contribute to heart attacks and strokes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A major new study suggests that many adults age 70 and older who have never experienced a heart attack or stroke may be able to stop taking statins without substantially increasing their short-term cardiovascular risks. However, the findings also point to a possible increase in risk over a longer period, making the decision more complicated than it initially appears.

The independent, preliminary research was presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, held November 6 through 9 in Chicago. The annual conference brings together cardiovascular researchers and healthcare professionals from around the world to share scientific discoveries, emerging evidence, and advances in clinical care.

It has been revealed that an estimated 25% of American adults have elevated levels of low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C), commonly called "bad cholesterol." When too much LDL cholesterol accumulates in the arteries, it can restrict blood flow and contribute to heart attacks and strokes. Statins are widely prescribed to lower cholesterol and reduce these risks, including in people who have never experienced a cardiovascular event. This preventive approach remains a central part of the American Heart Association's 2026 joint guideline on dyslipidemia.

Do Older Adults Need to Keep Taking Statins?

Although statins are an established treatment for reducing cardiovascular risk, questions remain about how much benefit they provide when people reach their 70s and beyond, particularly if they have never had a heart attack or stroke.

"While the Association's recent joint guideline recommends lifestyle and potentially medication for people with high LDL-C at younger ages to reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke, recent studies question the health benefits of continuing statins in the later decades of life," said study author Rita F. Redberg, M.D., M.Sc., FAHA, professor of cardiology and the Araxe Vilensky Endowed Chair in Cardiology at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine. "A few previous studies assessed the safety of discontinuing statins for primary prevention at age 70 and later, and they found no difference in mortality. One study suggested quality of life improvements after stopping statins. Whether it is safe to discontinue statins to prevent a first CVD event in the elderly remained unclear and the question we explored in our study.".

To investigate, researchers enrolled nearly 1,900 adults aged 70 and older who were taking statins specifically to prevent a first cardiovascular event. Every participant also had at least two chronic medical conditions, such as a history of cancer or lung disease.

Participants were divided into two groups. One group stopped taking statins, while the other continued their prescribed treatment. Researchers tracked their health for approximately two years, with additional follow-up extending as long as four years. They examined rates of heart attack, stroke, and death, along with changes in quality of life, muscle pain, falls, and muscle wasting (known as sarcopenia).

What Happened When Older Adults Stopped Statins?

The initial findings were largely reassuring. After approximately two years, participants who stopped taking statins did not experience a statistically significant increase in heart attacks, strokes, or deaths compared with those who remained on the medications.

Recent findings suggest that stopping treatment also did not produce measurable improvements in the other outcomes researchers examined. Quality of life, muscle discomfort, falls, and muscle wasting were similar in both groups.

There was, however, a small difference in cardiovascular outcomes. Over the first two years, the results indicated approximately one additional cardiovascular event for every 40 people who discontinued statins compared with those who continued treatment.

In a recent development, the longer follow-up revealed a more concerning pattern. Over a period of up to four years, 12.7% of participants who stopped statins experienced a heart attack, stroke, or death, compared with 9.2% of those who kept taking the medications.

Longer Follow-Up Reveals a Potential Risk.

Redberg explained that the higher rate of serious outcomes during the four-year follow-up represents a fresh finding in research on statin discontinuation among older adults. She suggested that the difference may have emerged because this trial included more participants and tracked them for a longer period than earlier studies.

Sources indicate that these results complicate the question of whether older adults should continue cholesterol treatment indefinitely. While the findings suggest that stopping statins may be a reasonable option for many people in this age group, they also indicate that remaining on treatment could offer some protection over time.

In a recent development, "This small, increased risk of cardiovascular events means that one cannot make a general recommendation about stopping statins in this patient population," she said. "There should be shared decision-making between the patient and the healthcare professional to know if it is appropriate for an individual to discontinue the medication. In general, however, discontinuation is safe for most people who are in this age group and without a previous CVD event.".

Study Design and Crucial Limitations.

Sources indicate that the trial involved 1,880 participants aged 70 and older (average age of 77; 53% men, and 47% women), all of whom had at least two chronic health conditions. Individuals with established cardiovascular disease or a previous cardiovascular event were not eligible to participate.

Researchers conducted the study between November 2021 and April 2026 across 24 medical centers in Switzerland, France, and the Netherlands. Of the participants, 938 were assigned to discontinue statins, while 942 were assigned to continue taking their medications.

In a recent development, throughout the trial and subsequent follow-up, researchers recorded heart attacks, acute ischemic strokes, and deaths from any cause. Participants also completed surveys assessing their overall quality of life, muscle pain, falls, and sarcopenia.

In a recent development, one limitation was that some participants did not remain in their originally assigned groups. Some people instructed to stop statins eventually resumed treatment, while others assigned to continue taking statins stopped using them. Altogether, approximately 14% of participants switched from their assigned treatment approach during the study.

To determine whether these changes affected the findings, the researchers performed several additional statistical analyses. The results remained unchanged.

Sources indicate that taken together, the findings suggest that discontinuing statins may be an option for many adults over 70 who have not previously experienced cardiovascular disease, especially when considering outcomes over the first two years. However, the higher rate of heart attacks, strokes, and deaths during longer follow-up underscores why stopping treatment should be an individualized decision made with a healthcare professional rather than a general recommendation for all older adults.

Forcing yourself to smile can actually make you miserable

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (997 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A smile might brighten your mood, but new research suggests that forcing yourself to smile over and over can have the opposite effect.
  • According to recent reports, for years, psychologist Nicholas Coles, Ph.D., studied evidence suggesting that even an artificial smile could make someone feel a little happier.
  • Sources indicate that "I used to work in customer service.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A smile might brighten your mood, but new research suggests that forcing yourself to smile over and over can have the opposite effect. When smiling becomes an obligation, especially one tied to financial pressure, it may actually leave people feeling less happy and more irritated.

According to recent reports, for years, psychologist Nicholas Coles, Ph.D., studied evidence suggesting that even an artificial smile could make someone feel a little happier. Yet those findings never quite matched his own experiences.

Sources indicate that "I used to work in customer service. I actually got written up for my inability to keep smiling at work at an unnamed theme park in Florida," laughed Coles, a professor of psychology at the University of Florida. "So I'm looking at all this evidence I had accrued so far that smiling boosts happiness and realizing it flies in the face of my own experiences in the world.".

That contradiction inspired Coles and his colleagues to investigate what happens when people must keep smiling, rather than simply trying it once. Their findings suggest an important distinction: A brief, intentional smile can provide a small emotional lift, but repeatedly putting on a smile under pressure can undermine happiness.

Testing How Forced Smiling Affects Happiness.

Recent findings suggest that to explore this difference, Coles worked with researchers Annabel Dang and Joao Francisco Goes Braga Takayanagi to design an experiment that more closely resembled the demands of customer service jobs. Their findings were published on October 1 in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology.

"We tried to combine the classic way of studying it in a lab with some extra ingredients that we might see in the real world. We told participants that we would pay them less if they weren't successfully smiling," Coles noted. "We also controlled the number of times they have to do it, because in customer service, every interaction is another faked smile.".

The online experiment initially enrolled 1,201 people, with data from 1,174 included in the final analysis. Participants were shown images designed to produce different emotional reactions. Some depicted appealing subjects, such as kittens and flowers, while others showed disturbing situations, including theft and mistreatment of animals.

During the experiment, participants either deliberately formed a smile or allowed their facial expressions to develop naturally. Depending on their assigned group, they completed the exercise once or repeated it 10 times.

To introduce an element of pressure, researchers warned half the participants that failing to follow the smiling instructions could cost them $2 from their $6 payment. However, nobody actually lost any money, and every participant received the full amount.

When Fake Smiles Start to Backfire.

Industry observers note that after completing each task, participants reported how happy they felt. The results highlighted that the emotional effects of smiling depended on how often people had to do it and whether they felt pressured.

In a recent development, when participants viewed unpleasant images, producing a single smile gave their mood a modest boost. This benefit appeared even among those who had been warned about a possible financial penalty. However, the positive effect weakened when smiling was repeated, and it disappeared when repeated smiles were combined with the threat of losing money.

In a recent development, the pattern was even more revealing when people looked at pleasant pictures. Smiling just once offered little additional happiness compared with allowing their faces to respond naturally. But when participants had to smile repeatedly or felt pressure to do so, their happiness ratings actually fell below those of people who responded naturally.

Further analysis revealed another unexpected consequence. In the pleasant picture conditions, forced smiling was also associated with increased irritation and anger.

"If you only force a smile once without any financial penalties, you can see the improvement in happiness. So what psychologists were seeing in their lab is right," he said. "But when you make it a little bit more like the real world, where you have to keep repeating it, and if you don't do it well, you get financial penalties, you see it completely reverse.".

The Hidden Emotional Cost of Smiling at Work.

These findings may help explain why expectations to appear cheerful throughout the workday can become frustrating rather than uplifting.

Industry observers note that the problem has already sparked controversy in the workplace. In recent years, Target faced widespread criticism over a policy requiring employees to smile when customers came within a specified distance. Although the policy was intended to encourage friendly interactions, Coles argues that such requirements can interfere with people's ability to express their emotions naturally.

The problem may extend beyond employees. Customers can also feel obligated to respond positively to friendliness that is being imposed rather than offered spontaneously. According to Coles, these expectations limit the emotional freedom of both sides of the interaction.

Could Trying Less to Be Happy Make Us Happier?

It has been revealed that after spending years investigating how people can improve their emotional well-being, Coles has begun considering a broader question. Rather than constantly searching for ways to increase happiness, might people be better off placing greater value on simply being content?

His research suggests that efforts to manufacture positive emotions do not always produce the intended results. Sometimes, trying too hard to appear happy can make the experience less pleasant.

"As a society, we have placed such an immense amount of emphasis on trying to make ourselves feel happier than we at the moment are," he mentioned, "much less emphasis on just being content with what we have.".

The Trump administration has agreed to withdraw its moratorium on upcoming broker enrollments, court documents show.

In a recent development, according to a filing submitted Thursday, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Service will published a withdrawal on the Federal Register. According to recent reports, the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America both sued over the regulation. NABIP argued that the moratorium would have a significant impact on licensed professionals operating in accordance with the law.

Recent findings suggest that per the document, that stay will remain in place until CMS publishes its withdrawal notice. Once that has been put forth, the plaintiffs will dismiss their complaints as moot. CMS also agreed not to take further action against agents and brokers during the current open enrollment period.

The moratorium, finalized in September, was a part the agency's broader efforts to root out fraud, waste and abuse on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

Recent findings suggest that UPDATED: Nov. 5 at 4:30 p.m. ET.

A federal court has granted a preliminary injunction to two key groups representing insurance brokers over the Trump administration's moratorium on newly introduced broker enrollments.

The District Court of Maryland issued the injunction after determining that the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America "have shown that they are likely to succeed on the merits of their claims under the Administrative Procedure Act.".

The court also stated that the organizations made clear they would likely suffer significant harm if the moratorium stays in place.

NABIP mentioned that the ruling means that it will restart training for new brokers beginning on Nov. 6.

In a recent development, "Today’s ruling is a significant victory for licensed agents and brokers and the consumers who rely on their expertise," remarked NABIP President Mychal Walker in an announcement (PDF). "With Open Enrollment already underway, every day matters.".

"Lifting the moratorium immediately and beginning training tomorrow will help affected professionals get to work assisting individuals and families in finding coverage that fits their needs and budgets," stated Walker.

NABIP initially sued on Oct. 15 to challenge the moratorium. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services instituted the moratorium in late September as part of its broader push to combat fraud on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

Sources indicate that PUBLISHED: Oct. 15 at 5:15 p.m. ET.

The National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals is suing the Trump administration over its moratorium on upcoming brokers entering the Affordable Care Act marketplaces.

The organization, the leading trade group for insurance brokers and agents, mentioned the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' moratorium impacts close to 19,000 brokers and agents who will be barred from registering ahead of open enrollment.

Industry observers note that CMS unveiled the moratorium in late September as part of its ongoing push to root out fraud, waste and abuse. In addition, the agency remarked it would terminate more than 200 agents and brokers that failed to comply with marketplace standards.

The agency remarked upcoming brokers and agents were disproportionately responsible for submitting inappropriate enrollments and engaging in behaviors at high risk for fraud.

In an announcement (PDF), NABIP states that it supports the broader effort to combat fraud, but that CMS' moratorium "threatens the livelihoods of thousands of legitimate, licensed professionals who have not been accused of fraud and limits consumers’ access to professional assistance as they navigate Open Enrollment.".

It has been revealed that the organization argues in the lawsuit that the rule instituting the moratorium violates both the Administrative Procedure Act and the Affordable Care Act. The regulation is unlawful as it is "arbitrary, capricious, and unsupported by sufficient evidence," NABIP said.

The 19,000 agents who would be barred from participating under the rule are part of a critical network of professionals who help consumers find coverage that meets their needs, the organization stated.

NABIP President Mychal Walker noted that CMS should look elsewhere in its fraud efforts.

Recent findings suggest that "The existence of fraud is not in dispute. NABIP has raised these concerns with CMS repeatedly and has offered concrete solutions to address them," Walker remarked in the announcement. "What is in dispute is whether the appropriate response is to exclude thousands of legitimate agents based solely on whether they registered last year, without any individualized evidence about them.".

"There is a better approach: target fraud where it occurs, strengthen the system’s security and hold bad actors accountable while preserving consumers’ access to trusted professionals," Walker continued.

CMS has taken steps to crack down on brokers as the agency views improper ACA enrollments as a key target in its fight against fraud. CMS officials have repeatedly raised concerns that people are enrolled in ACA prepares without their knowledge, or despite being deceased.

Earlier this week, the agency revealed it will purge 189,000 enrollees who are presently listed as enrolled in both ACA plans and other coverage, such as Medicaid or Medicare.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • That’s the question at the center of a growing debate in Clark County, NV, where water is scarce and locals are skeptical about a luxury development's proposal to create a massive water feature.
  • In a recent development, joel Laub and his partner, Randall Jones, began developing the Reserve at Red Rock Canyon in 2022, aiming to create a high-end luxury community amid the Nevada wilderness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that should a private developer have the ability to build a human-made pond in the middle of a drought-stricken region? What if that developer says that firefighters can access the pond to fight wildfires?

That’s the question at the center of a growing debate in Clark County, NV, where water is scarce and locals are skeptical about a luxury development's proposal to create a massive water feature.

In a recent development, joel Laub and his partner, Randall Jones, began developing the Reserve at Red Rock Canyon in 2022, aiming to create a high-end luxury community amid the Nevada wilderness. The Reserve is being built on 65 acres that were once home to the Bonnie Springs Ranch, a historic, Old West-themed family resort that once featured horseback riding and a small zoo.

It has been revealed that two-acre empty plots in the community start at $7.5 million. But that’s not what has the community up in arms. Instead, it’s what the Reserve is touting on its website: a large human-made pond in the middle of the property.

Industry observers note that to outsiders, it seems like just one feature in a long list of amenities. But for some locals in Clark County, which was declared a natural disaster area due to drought earlier this year, the pond seems like a slap in the face—even as the developers attempt to position it as a fire safety "dip pond.".

According to recent reports, “This little dip pond here is really fire safety as an afterthought, and I think that’s pretty obvious in terms of even their planning,” mentioned Sarah J. McCrea-Dameron, a Blue Diamond, NV, resident and former deputy fire chief from Las Vegas Fire & Rescue, at a zoning commission meeting this past week. “It’s not in an area that’s necessary, and it’s not the best use of that water and that precious resource for our community.“.

Industry observers note that the Reserve at Red Rock Canyon development sits within the Red Rock Canyon Conservation Area, an expansive 195,000-acre area within the Mojave Desert. Aztec sandstone foundations dating back to 180 million years can be found in the area, along with sea fossils and hundreds of local bird species. More than 3 million people visit the area each year.

Recent findings suggest that water for the area is supplied by the Colorado River. In recent years, the river and the several lakes it feeds have been pushed to the limit, as upcoming development, coupled with more frequent droughts, have strained resources.

The river doesn’t just supply necessary water to communities across the Southwest: It also produces much-needed hydropower for the region.

Earlier this year, Lake Powell, one of the lakes fed by the Colorado River, dropped to its lowest level in history, threatening to shut down the Glen Canyon Dam, which supplies power to Wyoming, Utah, Colorado, Latest Mexico, Arizona, Nevada, and Nebraska.

Communities around the Red Rock Canyon Conservation Area take the mantle of water conservation seriously. In fact, in 2020, the nearby community of Blue Diamond issued a temporary moratorium on “the issuance of additional water commitments” that remains in place.

Now, as the developers Laub and Jones offer unbuilt lots in their new development for $7.5 million, they are pitching the proposed pond as a neighborhood amenity.

“Paths and roads will meander past water features fed by the canyon’s natural springs,” the development’s website states.

It has been revealed that but those types of features are typically prohibited by Clark County’s Title 30, which governs building and development in the area. Title 30 right now prohibits the creation of human-made lakes of any size and water features greater than 10 square feet of surface area. So the developers stressed that the human-made pond would be fed via private water rights, and therefore not impede on community resources. Instead of using Colorado River resources, the project would be fed using groundwater.

Bob Gronauer, the developers' lawyer, said the water feature would be a “dip pond”—a water source for use by firefighting helicopters. Wildfires are a frequent problem in the region. In 2025 alone, there were 619 fires in the state, which destroyed more than 368,000 acres.

Industry observers note that in fact, the developers have already signed a use agreement with the Nevada Division of Forestry. The developers claimed the NDF came to them to ask them to create the pond, but the NDF said the developers approached them about the partnership, the Nevada Independent reported.

"We reached out to the Bureau of Land Management Red Rock management staff at the visitor center, Save Red Rock, Friends of Red Rock, as well as the Nature Conservancy Nevada immediately upon purchasing the property to work with them to make this development compatible with the Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area," Laub tells Realtor.com. (Laub is the chairman of the Nature Conservancy board.).

Laub states the idea for the dip pond actually came from the BLM.

"They asked if we could work with them on fire management in Red Rock Canyon, and would we consider providing water for firefighting. Of course our answer was yes. We have a 220,000-gallon water tank designed into our water system for supplying water to our fire hydrants, and we agreed to provide a fire hydrant for the BLM water tankers to fill up in the event of a wildfire," Laub continues.

"The ponds are designed to fit into the canyon ecosystem and look natural but also to be compatible with helicopter firefighting.".

Laub tells Realtor.com that they've already been testing the wells in the canyon, and "none of the testing results from these wells has indicated a draw down of significance from our use of the water system.".

He also notes that they purchased the water rights from Bonnie Springs Ranch, which had been in use for more than 60 years.

"The property has had ponds, streams, pools, and springs from the original ranch in 1952," he explains.

To expedite the creation of the dip pools, the developers proposed an amendment to Title 30 that would add language permitting “a body of water, served from standalone private water rights, within 1,000 feet of a National Conservation Area, intended for fire suppression and life safety purposes as agreed upon with a State or Federal Agency.”In October, Clark County Planning Commission's professional staff recommended denying the amendment.

"As proposed, there is no indication of how these water features would be designed, the capacity of these water features, or other potential uses for the stored water. The proliferation of non-essential water features will place an additional burden on the existing water supply," the staff recommendation read. "Furthermore, this request may encourage additional non-essential water features within residential and nonresidential development.".

In a recent development, however, the Planning Commission approved the amendment by a vote of 6-1. It then went to the Clark County Zoning Board for approval. On Wednesday night, during the public comment period of the meeting, around a dozen community members spoke out against the planned feature.

“You can design a decorative water feature and then call it a dip pond. You can offer to let the Forest Service use it knowing that they never will because of the way it’s designed and location, but that doesn’t make that decorative water feature a piece of critical fire infrastructure," said former Clark County Fire Capt. Erik Klausen.

“They’re trying to put a plastic fire helmet on this water feature and tell us it’s about public safety,” he continued.

At the end of the public comment period, all seven commissioners voted in favor of the proposed amendment, though, as Commissioner Justin Jones noted, the approval of the amendment does not mean the dip pond project has been approved.

Furthermore, noted Commissioner Marilyn Kirkpatrick, the project needs to be fit for purpose.

"If it's a fire-suppression pond, then it has to be a fire-suppression pond in my mind," remarked Kirkpatrick. "It should stay as a fire-supression pond, not as a recreational venue, not as irrigation, because that water is supposed to be there for a reason.".

Realtor.com has reached out to developer Jones and lawyer Gronauer for comment.

Crypto’s stablecoin market has shed $16 billion in a month, marking its sharpest contraction since the 2022 bear market. The retreat is hitting USDT and USDC hard, leaving fewer dollar-backed tokens circulating.

Total stablecoin market cap now stands at $283 billion, down more than 5% after losing $16.5 billion in a month. The decline puts the market under pressure just as crypto struggles to recover, with investors showing little appetite for buying the dip.

Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC account for most of the latest contraction. USDT is holding a market cap of $175.02 billion, down 4.3% over 30 days, while USDC fell to $68.58 billion, losing 5% during the same period. Together, the two stablecoins represent 86% of the entire market.

In a recent development, the contraction also extends beyond dollar-backed tokens. Sky Dollar’s USDS supply dropped 22.32% over 30 days, while Ethena’s USDe expanded 4.36%. The gap indicates that some are still moving between stablecoin products.

CryptoQuant data points the same way. CryptoQuant data published on November 11 showed USDT market cap had fallen $6.6 billion over 60 days through November 7. It was more than twice the $3.2 billion decline recorded after FTX collapsed in November 2022.

Discover: The Best Token Presales.

Recent findings suggest that the current contraction brings back an ugly history. Stablecoin supply reached $161.5 billion in March 2022 before entering a prolonged decline. Terra’s UST collapse accelerated the withdrawal of capital, with nearly $30 billion disappearing from stablecoin supply in June alone.

That monthly decline was almost twice the latest $16.5 billion contraction. Back in 2022, the damage continued into the following year. By September 2023, aggregate stablecoin supply had fallen by 26% from its March 2022 peak, a contraction of $43 billion.

Bitcoin endured a similar period of weakness. After reaching nearly $69,000 in November 2021, BTC eventually plunged to around $15,500 in November 2022. Stablecoin supply continued shrinking even after the initial market shock initiated by Terra. Crypto’s liquidity problems then became a prolonged market condition.

Yet, in 2023, not every stablecoin experienced the same fate. USDT supply rose $13.3 billion from its November 2022 lows, while USDC lost $16.7 billion. During that period, investors were not simply abandoning every stablecoin. Some were moving toward Tether as the market reassessed issuers and available returns.

This time, arguably, the stablecoin contraction is happening against a different market backdrop. Crypto traders have fewer reasons to keep large amounts of capital parked in stablecoins when Bitcoin and major altcoins struggle to attract buyers. Some holders may be redeeming their tokens for traditional dollars, while others are moving into interest-bearing assets outside crypto.

A shrinking stablecoin market does not mean every dollar has left digital assets. But the simultaneous decline in USDT and USDC supply makes the latest contraction harder to dismiss as simple rotation between issuers.

A crypto recovery needs buyers willing to commit fresh capital, and stablecoins have historically provided traders with an immediate way to enter the market.
