💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that incident remediation company Resolve AI Inc.
  • Industry observers note that the upcoming model, announced Wednesday, reflects the firm’s argument that while AI has transformed how software gets written, it has barely touched how software gets run.
  • In a recent development, SRE-1 is a 27 billion-parameter model built on open weights and trained by a team of 16 AI researchers over a final run of 7.4 days on up to 512 graphics processing units.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:11 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Industry observers note that incident remediation company Resolve AI Inc. has unveiled the launch of SRE-1, a newly introduced model that has been trained to find the root cause of production alerts, and Primary On-call, a new service that puts its artificial intelligence agents on call ahead of human engineers.

Industry observers note that the upcoming model, announced Wednesday, reflects the firm’s argument that while AI has transformed how software gets written, it has barely touched how software gets run. According to Resolve AI, production has no public training corpus to match the published code that models learned from, as incidents at each company stay private.

In a recent development, SRE-1 is a 27 billion-parameter model built on open weights and trained by a team of 16 AI researchers over a final run of 7.4 days on up to 512 graphics processing units. Measured on the same incidents before and after training, which used reinforcement learning alone, the pass rate for a single investigation rose from 6.9% to 38.8%.

Resolve AI used Snowflake Inc.’s Cortex Training, a serverless service for customizing open-weight models, to build SRE-1. Snowflake Senior Vice President of Engineering Vivek Raghunathan mentioned Resolve AI was the first design partner for the service.

In testing on 49 difficult live production cases, each run five times, an ensemble of five SRE-1 investigations matched the strongest frontier model tested at a lower cost, according to the company. Resolve AI also benchmarked its complete system on 178 production alert investigations, solving about twice as many incidents as general-purpose coding agents.

According to recent reports, primary On-call puts that research to work on the critical path. Each page is investigated across telemetry, infrastructure, code and operational knowledge, according to the company. Depending on what it finds, the agent can close the alert, mitigate the problem where a team’s policies permit or escalate to a human. Once it has acted, the agent checks the fix against the production baseline, monitoring it until recovery holds.

According to recent reports, the agent also links related alerts and investigations into a shared view of each underlying problem. For teams wary of handing over the pager straight away, Resolve AI offers a shadow mode that records the call the agent would have made on each page.

Up to 80% of paged alerts in production are remarked to be handled by Primary On-call without escalation. Customers have reported a tenfold improvement in mean time to resolution, along with root-cause accuracy of up to 95%, according to Resolve AI.

Recent findings suggest that salesforce Inc. is among the early customers. Bhupesh Patel, a software engineering principal architect at Salesforce, mentioned that in the first few weeks of dark launch testing, the agent closed more than 70% of the CRM Analytics team’s paging alerts “without waking an engineer.”.

In a recent development, “No engineering team can keep up with how fast code and patches land in production,” said Resolve AI Chief Executive Spiros Xanthos. “The answer is agents that are accurate and fast enough to sit on the critical path, and that takes a model built for production.”.

Primary On-call is now generally available. Access to SRE-1 is limited to Resolve AI’s own platform.

Resolve AI is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised more than $190 million to date, including a $40 million extension to its Series A round in April, led by DST Global and Salesforce Ventures, that valued the company at $1.5 billion. Notable customers include Coinbase Global Inc., DoorDash Inc., Figma Inc., MSCI Inc., Nasdaq Inc., SAP SE and Zscaler Inc.

#122084. Latest Update: MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1272 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1272 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that while we go about our daily activities, the brain gradually accumulates waste, including lactic acid and proteins that are no longer useful.
  • In a recent development, researchers at MIT have now discovered a way to make these fluid waves stronger using brief pulses of a gentle sound called "pink noise." When delivered at carefully chosen moments during sleep, the sounds amplify slow electrical waves in the brain.
  • Industry observers note that the finding opens up intriguing possibilities for improving brain health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that while we go about our daily activities, the brain gradually accumulates waste, including lactic acid and proteins that are no longer useful. Sleep provides an important opportunity to clear away these substances. As we rest, waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) move through the brain, helping remove waste and maintain healthy brain function.

In a recent development, researchers at MIT have now discovered a way to make these fluid waves stronger using brief pulses of a gentle sound called "pink noise." When delivered at carefully chosen moments during sleep, the sounds amplify slow electrical waves in the brain. Those stronger electrical signals, in turn, produce larger waves of CSF.

Industry observers note that the finding opens up intriguing possibilities for improving brain health. Scientists want to determine whether increasing this fluid movement could sharpen thinking, strengthen memory, or slow neurodegenerative diseases associated with the accumulation of damaging proteins, including amyloid beta.

Industry observers note that "We found that we were able to increase the size of the CSF flow wave during sleep, which as far as we know, there hasn't been a method to do before. Now that we can enhance CSF flow during sleep in healthy adults, we're really excited to bring this technology to clinical populations to see what effects we can have," notes Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Lewis led the research as senior author. The findings were published in Science Translational Medicine, with Joshua Levitt serving as lead author. Levitt recently completed his PhD at Boston University and previously worked as a visiting graduate student in Lewis' laboratory.

How Sleep Helps the Brain Remove Waste.

Industry observers note that cerebrospinal fluid is a transparent liquid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord, providing protection against physical injury. It also supports brain function by transporting nutrients, including glucose, and carrying away waste released by brain cells as they consume energy.

Sources indicate that in 2019, Lewis demonstrated that functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) could be used to observe the movement of CSF into and out of the brain during sleep. Her team found that this movement closely follows slow electrical brain waves, which are especially prominent during deep sleep.

Industry observers note that building on that discovery, the researchers wanted to understand whether deliberately strengthening these electrical waves would also increase the movement of CSF. Earlier experiments had shown that sounds presented at precisely the right moment could enhance slow brain waves.

Industry observers note that "You can make more of these electrical slow waves through an auditory stimulus, if it comes at just the right time. Similar to a child on a swing, if you push them when they're at the right moment in their movement, you can make that swing go farther," Lewis says. "The challenge is: How do you find just the right time?".

How Pink Noise Amplifies Brain Waves.

In a recent development, to test the idea, the team used extremely short bursts of pink noise, each lasting just 50 milliseconds. Pink noise contains the full range of frequencies that humans can hear, much like white noise. However, its lower frequencies are more prominent, while higher frequencies are quieter. The result is a softer, more balanced sound reminiscent of steady rainfall or a waterfall heard from a distance.

Timing was essential. The researchers needed to deliver each burst of sound when a sleeping participant's slow brain waves reached their peak. To identify those moments, they monitored electrical activity using EEG while simultaneously measuring CSF movement with fMRI.

It has been revealed that combining the two measurements created a technical obstacle. The powerful magnetic fields used in fMRI interfere with EEG recordings, making it difficult to detect the brain's electrical signals accurately and quickly enough to synchronize the sound.

Sources indicate that the team addressed this problem by creating a method that removes interference from EEG signals in less than 100 milliseconds. They also designed an algorithm capable of predicting when the next slow wave peak would occur, compensating for the small delay introduced by processing the signals. Together, these advances made it possible to play each burst of pink noise at the intended moment.

Stronger Brain Cleaning Waves During Sleep.

The researchers tested their approach in 14 healthy volunteers. They found that the carefully timed sounds increased the size of both the brain's slow electrical waves and the accompanying CSF waves. Importantly, the sounds were quiet enough that they did not wake the participants.

It has been revealed that the brain scans also helped explain how the process works. Slow electrical waves were associated with blood vessels narrowing and widening, creating a pumping effect that pushes CSF out of the brain. These slow waves occur during non-REM sleep and become increasingly pronounced as sleep deepens.

In a recent development, by enhancing the electrical waves, the researchers were able to strengthen the fluid movement associated with the brain's natural waste removal process. However, the study did not directly establish whether the stronger CSF waves actually removed more waste or improved sleep quality.

Could Pink Noise Improve Sleep and Help Fight Alzheimer's?

It has been revealed that the researchers now want to investigate whether increasing CSF flow leads to more refreshing, restorative sleep, particularly for people who struggle with insomnia. Another major goal is to determine whether the technique can improve the brain's ability to clear harmful substances.

According to recent reports, this possibility is especially relevant to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia, which are associated with the accumulation of abnormal proteins in the brain. If stronger CSF movement ultimately translates into more effective waste removal, the approach could offer a new way to address one of the biological processes involved in these conditions.

Industry observers note that "Brain waste clearance is really important for Alzheimer's and other forms of dementia, which are caused, in part, by the buildup of molecules like amyloid and tau in the brain. If we can improve brain waste clearance, we may be able to help prevent the buildups of these plaques that lead to disease," Levitt says.

The technology could eventually become accessible outside research laboratories. Levitt has launched a firm that aims to develop a home device, potentially in the form of a headband, that would deliver sound at the appropriate moments during sleep to increase CSF flow.

For now, the results demonstrate that a simple auditory stimulus, when precisely synchronized with brain activity, can alter the fluid waves associated with the brain's nighttime cleaning process. Whether those changes can translate into better sleep, stronger memory, or protection against neurodegenerative disease remains an vital question for future studies.

The research received funding from a McKnight Scholar Award, a Sloan Fellowship, a Pew Biomedical Scholars Award, the Simons Foundation Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, the MIT EECS Transformative Research Fund, the National Institutes of Health, the Corundum Convergence Institute, and the Panasonic Well Fellowship for AI and Wellness.

Wedding bells are ringing for Miley Cyrus and her fiancé, Maxx Morando.

The rockers are planning to say “I do” in a ceremony in Southern California this weekend, according to a TMZ source.

The news of their engagement was first confirmed in September 2025, after Cyrus was seen wearing a sparkling engagement ring as they posed together on the red carpet at the premiere of “Avatar: Fire and Ash.”.

In a recent development, cyrus, 33, and Morando, 28, have been linked since the summer of 2021. In a British Vogue cover interview, the “Flowers” singer recalled their introduction, explaining, “We got put on a blind date.”.

She then provided a key clarifying detail, noting, “Well, it was blind for me and not really for him. I thought, ‘The worst that can happen is I leave.’”.

It’s safe to say the date was a success, with their love story blossoming over the last four years.

Almost immediately, they began collaborating together professionally, with Cyrus telling Vogue Morando was one of her “favorite emerging artists,” having designed sustainable looks for her to wear during her various appearances in music festivals in 2021.

Later that year, Morando’s band, Liily, performed as part of “Miley’s Newly introduced Year’s Eve Party,” where the “Hannah Montana” star rang in the New Year with an NBC special.

He’s even collaborated on some of Cyrus’s most recent music, and in a Harper’s Bazaar interview, she explained the significance of bringing a romantic partner into her professional sphere.

Industry observers note that “I worked with my dad forever. That’s how me and my ex-husband met each other,” she noted. “I’ve always worked with the people that I love. And Maxx just inspires me so much.”.

While Morando appears to be quite private in regards to his personal life, he has publicly supported his soon-to-be wife at a handful of public events, including movie premieres and award reveals.

Industry observers note that A few years into their relationship, the nearlyweds took a major leap. A People magazine source confirmed they had moved in together in February 2024.

“She is very happy with him,” the source revealed. “Miley has changed a lot in the past couple of years. She seems more calm and harmonious. Everyone loves Maxx. He’s a great guy. She is very happy with him. He’s private and doesn’t like being in the press. It’s been good for her.”.

Cyrus shared what it’s like to live with her fiance in a September 2026 chat on the Zane Lowe Show, where she gushed that even life’s most mundane tasks are more fun with Morando around.

According to recent reports, I think that’s the thing that maybe generations prior didn’t teach us, that marriage doesn’t need to be a prison. It can actually be a playground,” she said. “It’s just living with a best friend. And that’s what it is.”.

In 2024, an Us magazine source confirmed that although “Miley owns a number of properties,” the lovebirds are “staying at her home in Malibu,” which was described as a “huge mansion overlooking the water in a gated community.”.

In a recent development, although Cyrus also has homes in Studio City, Hidden Hills, and her home state of Tennessee, the couple reportedly adores the Malibu home’s proximity to the sea. Apparently, they “spend a lot of time on the private beach together.”.

Cyrus has a long history of living in Malibu—and even has a song named after the coastal locale.

Industry observers note that back in 2016, she paid $2.5 million for a gorgeous midcentury modern home in the area. At the time, she shared the 1,385-square-foot dwelling with her now-ex-husband, Liam Hemsworth. The former couple used it as a creative studio and guest house.

The funky home was perched on a two-acre property with lots of lush greenery, which could be peacefully enjoyed from the terrace of the primary bedroom, according to Architectural Digest.

The singer and “The Hunger Games” star would call another Malibu mansion their home, however—a $6.8 million property Hemsworth had purchased in 2014, which was tragically destroyed by the 2018 Wolsey Fire just weeks before their wedding.

Sources indicate that the sprawling property was more than just a home. It also housed Rainbowland, her personal recording studio.

Miley reflected on the tragedy in 2025, telling People, “When my house burned down, that was the biggest blessing I’ve ever had in my life, actually.”.

She explained that after “losing everything,” having the opportunity “to rebuild” inspired her to be more “purposeful” when carefully selecting fresh belongings.

Cyrus and Hemsworth separated in August 2019, and their divorce was finalized in January 2020.

In the months following the split, Cyrus offloaded the guesthouse at a loss in an off-market transaction for $1.7 million, and Hemsworth sold the wildfire-damaged property for $3.6 million.

It wouldn’t be too long before the “Black Mirror” actress would find herself back in Malibu. She snapped up a $7.9 million Mediterranean mansion in the city in 2022, which is reportedly where she and Morando live now.

The 1999-built property is on a 1.48-acre-lot in a gated community, which affords lots of privacy.

It’s truly a resort-like retreat, with a pool and spa in the backyard surrounded by soaring palm trees.

Indoors, an open-proposal layout boasts tall ceilings and glass sliding doors that connect the serene space to the equally-tranquil landscape.

The massive primary suite provides striking panoramic views of the beach, and has a lounge space, a fireplace, and a balcony.

Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

📅 07 Jun 2023 | ⏱️ 4 min read (731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtybiznews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients.
  • Industry observers note that the first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience.
  • Industry observers note that the headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

Industry observers note that the first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

Industry observers note that the headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

Recent findings suggest that when writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Sources indicate that storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

Industry observers note that in the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

Sources indicate that to encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

According to recent reports, an effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt owners to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

In a recent development, writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1684 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the heart gets older, inflammation increases, but scientists have not fully understood where these changes occur or which parts of the organ are most affected.
  • According to recent reports, in a study of mouse hearts published in Aging Cell, the researchers discovered that signs of inflammation and tissue scarring were especially concentrated around the aortic valves and aortic root.
  • Recent findings suggest that "Some of the markers associated with inflammaging were there from the very beginning in young hearts, but they were focused specifically in areas no one had defined before, in the valves and the aorta rather than in muscle tissue," noted study author Nadia Rosenthal, scientific director at JAX.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the heart gets older, inflammation increases, but scientists have not fully understood where these changes occur or which parts of the organ are most affected. Researchers at The Jackson Laboratory (JAX) have now uncovered a surprising pattern: Certain regions of the heart appear to be hotspots for aging-related inflammation, offering latest clues about how the heart changes over time.

According to recent reports, in a study of mouse hearts published in Aging Cell, the researchers discovered that signs of inflammation and tissue scarring were especially concentrated around the aortic valves and aortic root. These areas contain immune cells and connective tissue cells whose interactions change with age, potentially affecting the surrounding heart muscle. The findings provide a newly introduced picture of cardiac aging and could guide future efforts to understand cardiovascular disease.

Recent findings suggest that "Some of the markers associated with inflammaging were there from the very beginning in young hearts, but they were focused specifically in areas no one had defined before, in the valves and the aorta rather than in muscle tissue," noted study author Nadia Rosenthal, scientific director at JAX. "We really have to think of aging as something that is not linear, because just like we know that people don't age at the same rate, what we know now is that organs and tissues don't age at the same rate either, even within one individual.".

Industry observers note that much of the previous research on heart aging has centered on cardiac muscle, particularly the left ventricle. This chamber performs the essential task of pumping blood into the aorta and throughout the body. By studying the heart as a whole, rather than concentrating primarily on its muscle, the JAX team uncovered important changes in other tissues and the ways their cells interact.

According to recent reports, "The valves and the major blood vessels are parts often thought of as plumbing rather than the main engine, but this is a very complicated little machine," Rosenthal noted. "It turns out they're home to many of the cells we're interested in, and that's where some of the most important aging-related signals were concentrated.".

Mapping Hidden Hotspots of Heart Aging.

Growing older is the single greatest risk factor for cardiovascular disease, yet many of the cellular processes responsible for the heart's decline remain poorly understood. One challenge is that mammalian heart muscle cells have very little ability to regenerate or replace themselves. To investigate what happens as the heart ages, Rosenthal and her colleagues used advanced techniques that allowed them to study thousands of individual cells from young and old mice while also identifying their locations within the heart.

In a recent development, scientists already know that aging is accompanied by a persistent, low level of inflammation throughout the body. Earlier studies have found similar changes in the heart, including an increase in immune cells that regulate inflammatory activity (macrophages) and cells that produce and maintain connective tissue and contribute to scar formation (fibroblasts).

The upcoming analysis showed that aging macrophages became more active in genes involved in inflammation and changes to tissue structure. Fibroblasts, meanwhile, increasingly displayed molecular characteristics associated with fibrosis (or scarring). Crucially, the researchers went beyond identifying which genes were active. They also mapped the locations of these cells, making it possible to see how different regions of the heart change as they grow older.

This approach revealed that inflammation and fibrosis (or scarring) were not distributed uniformly. Instead, the strongest signals appeared around the heart valves and aortic root. The researchers believe these regions may act as key centers of cardiac aging, where changes in supporting cells could influence the health of nearby heart muscle.

According to recent reports, "To keep muscle cells happy, the other cells in the heart have to continue supporting them throughout life," Rosenthal said. "What this study does, for the first time, is provide a comprehensive picture of how those support cells, particularly fibroblasts and macrophages, change with age and contribute to what we call inflammaging.".

Surprising Signs of Aging in Young Hearts.

Industry observers note that another unexpected discovery challenged assumptions about how scientists identify aging cells. The team examined molecular markers frequently associated with cellular senescence, a state in which cells permanently lose the ability to divide, often because of aging or stress. As senescent cells accumulate, they can contribute to ongoing inflammation, tissue damage, and diseases associated with older age.

In a recent development, surprisingly, some of these supposedly age-related markers were already present in young mouse hearts. Their presence suggests that the markers alone cannot reliably establish whether a cell has entered senescence, and that their meaning may depend on where they appear and the condition of the surrounding tissue.

"What surprised us was that some of these markers that have been associated with aging were already present in young hearts. They weren't where anyone expected to find them, and that forced us to rethink what those markers are telling us," Rosenthal remarked. "That turns the usual interpretation of cardiac aging on its ear because these markers alone don't mean a cell is senescent. There's nothing senescent about a six-month-old mouse heart.".

The researchers also identified genes that became more active with age and were especially prominent in the same regions. Among them were Ccl8, which helps transmit inflammatory signals, and Cdkn1a (also known as p21), a gene widely used as an indicator of cellular senescence. Their locations provided further evidence that the valves and aortic root may be particularly vital areas for understanding how the heart ages.

"We're not talking about single genes. We're talking about an entire conversation between immune cells and fibroblasts. As the heart ages, the way those cells communicate changes, and that shift appears to be linked to the inflammation and tissue remodeling we see in older hearts," Rosenthal said.

Male and Female Hearts Show Different Aging Patterns.

The study uncovered another key distinction: Aging did not produce exactly the same molecular changes in male and female mouse hearts.

In males, aging fibroblasts showed stronger connections to biological processes associated with fibrosis. In females, the corresponding changes were more closely related to pathways involved in heart development and protein production.

Recent findings suggest that rosenthal noted that these differences may offer clues about cardiovascular aging in humans. Heart disease tends to become more common in women after menopause, while its development in men generally follows a more gradual pattern. The distinct cellular changes observed in male and female mice could help researchers investigate the biological processes behind these differences.

According to recent reports, however, the results describe differences in molecular activity, not demonstrated differences in heart function or disease risk. Further research will be needed to determine how these patterns influence cardiovascular health.

In a recent development, to explore whether their findings might also apply to people, the team compared the mouse results with previously published data from human hearts. Several molecular processes associated with aging, including pathways involved in responding to cellular stress, appeared in both species. This overlap suggests that at least some of the biological changes identified in mice may also be relevant to human heart aging.

"Our findings change the focus from aging across the entire heart to specific anatomical hotspots, helping us better understand how inflammation and fibrosis are connected and which regions of the heart are involved in the aging process," said study author Amalia Sintou, a postdoctoral associate at JAX.

Could These Discoveries Help Protect Aging Hearts?

Although the research does not yet identify a latest treatment, it offers scientists a more detailed understanding of where aging-related changes occur and which cells are involved. By revealing these cellular patterns, the findings could help guide future studies aimed at reducing cardiovascular decline, maintaining healthy heart function, and improving health later in life.

Rosenthal's team is now examining whether exercise, diet, and disease alter the interactions between immune cells and connective tissue cells. The researchers hope to distinguish the normal effects of aging from changes that may leave the heart increasingly vulnerable to cardiovascular problems.

Recent findings suggest that the experimental design also helped the team isolate aging itself as a contributing factor. Because the mice lived under the same conditions and received the same diet, the researchers could investigate age-related changes without the additional variation introduced by different environments or eating habits.

It has been revealed that "Valve replacement is common in older adults, and one of the big questions is how much of the underlying damage is driven by aging itself," remarked study author Aleksandra Aljakna Khan, a postdoctoral associate at JAX. "Because all of the mice in our study lived in the same environment and ate the same diet, we were able to isolate the effects of aging and show that aging alone can initiate some of these changes in the valves and aorta.".

Together, the findings suggest that understanding heart aging requires looking beyond the muscle responsible for pumping blood. The valves, major blood vessels, and supporting cells may play a much larger role than previously recognized. Learning how these structures change and communicate over time could eventually help scientists identify ways to preserve cardiovascular health as people age.

Research Funding and Study Authors.

The research received funding from the NIH Common Fund through The Jackson Laboratory Senescence Tissue Mapping Center (JAX-Sen TMC U54 AG079753). Additional support came from JAX's National Cancer Institute-designated Cancer Center (P30 CA034196).

Additional authors from The Jackson Laboratory included Yue Zhao, Antonios Somarakis, Harshpreet Chandok, Juliana Alcoforado Diniz, Ramalakshmi Ramasamy, Gretchen T. Clark, Brian S. White, Paul Robson, Ron Korstanje, and J. Matthew Mahoney. Leon Frommer and Sikander Hayat of RWTH Aachen University also contributed to the study.

Despite posting a solid earnings beat, Elastic sees its stock slide on rough guidance

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (975 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elastic N.V.’s stock was trending lower in late trading today after the enterprise search software firm reported earnings and revenue that beat Wall Street’s expectations but disappointed with guidance that came in below forecasts.
  • Recent findings suggest that the company reported second-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of 94 cents per share, easily beating the analyst consensus estimate of 81 cents.
  • The results helped Elastic bounce back into profitability.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:33 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Elastic N.V.’s stock was trending lower in late trading today after the enterprise search software firm reported earnings and revenue that beat Wall Street’s expectations but disappointed with guidance that came in below forecasts.

Recent findings suggest that the company reported second-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of 94 cents per share, easily beating the analyst consensus estimate of 81 cents. Revenue rose 17%, to $496 million, surpassing the Street’s target of $487 million.

The results helped Elastic bounce back into profitability. Its net income for the quarter came to $171 million, rebounding from a loss of $51.3 million in the same period one year ago.

However, investors were less than impressed with the manufacturer’s guidance. For the quarter in progress, Elastic said it’s looking for earnings of between 90 cents and 92 cents per share on sales of $507.5 million to $508.5 million. That’s some way below the Street’s targets of 95 cents in earnings and $517.6 million in revenue. The company is not helped by the weak Euro, with currency conversions likely to cause a $4.5 million headwind on revenue in the quarter.

The full-year picture is not much better, as Elastic forecast annual sales of between $2 billion and $2.01 billion compared with the Street’s model of $2.01 billion.

According to recent reports, netherlands-based Elastic is one of Europe’s most successful software companies. It’s the developer of the popular open-source enterprise search platform Elasticsearch, which is used by thousands of businesses all over the world. The base platform is free to download and use, with Elastic making money by selling a special cloud-hosted version that ships with premium features not available in the open edition. The firm also sells application observability and security tools.

In the last couple of years, Elastic has tried to cash in on the artificial intelligence boom by positioning Elasticsearch as a useful cog in the wheel that feeds real-time data into large language models to provide them with business context. A key capability is Elastic Context Engine, which gathers, structures, and serves business-specific context to AI agents so they can make accurate decisions with fewer tokens and lower latency.

More recently, the manufacturer has built AI-native products including AlertZero, which enables enterprises to orchestrate teams of autonomous security agents that automate tasks around data protection and threat hunting.

According to recent reports, elastic Chief Executive Ash Kulkarni (pictured) said he’s excited about the potential of those newly introduced capabilities to drive significant revenue over time. “Elastic delivered another strong quarter, beating guidance across all key metrics,” he said. “Our strong results reflect expanding customer adoption and position us well to continue our strong execution in the back half of fiscal 2027.”.

According to recent reports, unfortunately for Kulkarni, investors didn’t seem to share his enthusiasm. The market was clearly expecting trouble on the horizon in the hours before the firm published its report, as its stock declined 8% during regular trading. Once the results were out, it fell another 8% after-hours. That means Elastic’s stock is now up just over 1% in the year to date.

Recent findings suggest that elastic’s stock had rallied more than 150% between April and October, but virtually all of those gains have now been erased. Prior to today, the shares had already lost more than 20% this month amid broader concerns about the AI industry. Some investors continue to worry about the potential of AI technology to challenge the business models of software companies.

Elastic is trying to sidestep those concerns by de-emphasizing search and observability and moving towards runtime context, model evaluation and AI operations, but investors are not yet convinced it will be able to do so successfully, Constellation Research analyst Michael Ni told SiliconANGLE.

It has been revealed that “While Elastic is showing good underlying momentum, the Street wants to see more proof that its re-acceleration can hold,” Ni remarked. “The next few quarters will show whether the broader platform story translates into sustainable growth or remains ahead of the numbers.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A surprising discovery involving vitamin B12 could open latest possibilities for understanding and potentially treating rare genetic disorders.
  • The findings center on a cellular process called RNA splicing, which helps prepare the genetic instructions cells use to produce proteins.
  • Mutations in genes responsible for splicing can cause conditions such as Verheij syndrome.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A surprising discovery involving vitamin B12 could open latest possibilities for understanding and potentially treating rare genetic disorders. Researchers found that the vitamin can correct developmental problems in tiny worms carrying a genetic mutation associated with Verheij syndrome, a rare human condition that causes developmental delays, impaired growth, and short stature.

The findings center on a cellular process called RNA splicing, which helps prepare the genetic instructions cells use to produce proteins. During splicing, unnecessary portions of messenger RNA are removed, and the remaining sections are joined together in the correct order. When this process goes wrong, it can disrupt essential cellular functions and contribute to serious developmental disorders.

Mutations in genes responsible for splicing can cause conditions such as Verheij syndrome. To better understand the effects of these genetic changes, scientists investigated how a related mutation affects growth and metabolism in a laboratory model.

Vitamin B12 Reverses Developmental Defects in Worms.

According to recent reports, the discovery emerged from experiments involving C. elegans, a tiny roundworm commonly used in biological research. The researchers were initially searching for previously unknown genes that influence lifespan when they began examining a mutation in a gene involved in RNA splicing. The same gene is associated with Verheij syndrome in humans.

Worms carrying the mutation developed problems resembling important features of the human disorder. Their growth slowed considerably, and they remained smaller than normal.

To investigate why this happened, the scientists conducted genetic screens and analyzed the worms' metabolism. They discovered that the mutation disrupted specific metabolic pathways that depend on vitamin B12 and are essential for healthy growth and normal cellular activity.

According to recent reports, the researchers then tested whether providing additional vitamin B12 could counteract these changes. Remarkably, the treatment restored the affected metabolic processes to normal and corrected the developmental abnormalities associated with the mutation.

Recent findings suggest that "We were surprised to find that a change in a fundamental process of RNA processing had such a targeted effect on vitamin B12-dependent metabolism," states Jonathan Kölschbach, first author of the study. "Even more exciting was that we were able to largely correct the consequences of this change in the worm model using vitamin B12.".

Could Vitamin B12 Help Treat a Rare Genetic Disorder?

In a recent development, to explore whether their findings might also apply to people, the researchers examined publicly available datasets from human cells. They also worked with Hormos Dafsari, a neuropediatrician at the University Hospital Cologne, to collect blood samples from patients diagnosed with Verheij syndrome.

These investigations uncovered evidence of similar metabolic changes in humans, suggesting that the vitamin B12-related pathways affected in the worms may also play a role in the human disorder.

Although the results are promising, researchers have not yet established whether vitamin B12 supplementation can improve symptoms in people with Verheij syndrome. Additional studies will be necessary to determine whether the benefits observed in worms can be translated into a treatment for patients.

According to recent reports, the discovery also raises a broader possibility. Metabolic disruptions may contribute more substantially to diseases caused by faulty RNA splicing than scientists previously recognized. Understanding these connections could help researchers identify new therapeutic strategies, potentially extending beyond Verheij syndrome to other rare genetic conditions.

Recent findings suggest that "Our study is a good example of how basic research on model organisms can provide new insights into human diseases," claims Adam Antebi, Director at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing and lead author of the study. "A fundamental biological question can thus give rise to a new approach that could also become medically relevant in the long term.".

Newly introduced wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1043 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new wearable patch could offer a surprisingly simple way to improve one of the most important stages of sleep, without relying on medication or surgery.
  • Known as NEUSLeeP, the soft patch attaches to the skin and combines ultrasound stimulation with electrodes that monitor brain activity in real time.
  • Industry observers note that REM sleep, short for rapid eye movement sleep, is the stage when most vivid dreaming occurs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new wearable patch could offer a surprisingly simple way to improve one of the most important stages of sleep, without relying on medication or surgery. Developed by researchers led by the University of Texas at Austin, the device uses gentle ultrasound waves to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, helping people enter REM sleep sooner and spend more time in this restorative stage.

Known as NEUSLeeP, the soft patch attaches to the skin and combines ultrasound stimulation with electrodes that monitor brain activity in real time. This allows researchers to influence brain regions involved in sleep while simultaneously tracking how the brain responds.

Industry observers note that REM sleep, short for rapid eye movement sleep, is the stage when most vivid dreaming occurs. It also plays an vital role in processing emotions, consolidating memories, and adapting to stress. Disturbances in this stage of sleep have been associated with several mental health conditions, making it an important target for upcoming treatments.

It has been revealed that "This is the first time we've been able to noninvasively target deep brain regions involved in REM sleep, while simultaneously monitoring brain activity," noted Kai Wing "Kevin" Tang, a recent UT biomedical engineering Ph.D. graduate who led the research effort.

It has been revealed that "Our skin-attached NEUSLeeP patch opens up latest possibilities for understanding sleep and treating sleep disorders in home settings," added Huiliang "Evan" Wang, assistant professor in the Cockrell School of Engineering's Department of Biomedical Engineering. Wang supervised Tang's research and served as the principal investigator (PI) overseeing the project.

Sleep Patch Helps People Reach REM Sleep 43 Minutes Faster.

The early results suggest that the technology can make a measurable difference in how people experience REM sleep.

In a study involving 28 participants, published in Nature Communications, people using the patch entered REM sleep an average of 43 minutes sooner and spent approximately 16 additional minutes in that stage.

These improvements were observed in both healthy sleepers and participants experiencing certain sleep difficulties. The volunteers also reported that the patch was comfortable to wear, with minimal adverse effects.

Recent findings suggest that unlike medications that affect the body more broadly, NEUSLeeP is designed to deliver stimulation to specific brain regions involved in sleep regulation. It uses ultrasound, a form of sound energy with frequencies beyond human hearing, to reach areas beneath the surface of the brain without requiring an invasive procedure.

The findings are encouraging, although the relatively small study means that larger trials will be needed to determine how consistently the technology works and whether its benefits persist over time.

Potential Benefits for Stress and Emotional Health.

The researchers also found evidence that the patch's effects may extend beyond increasing REM sleep.

Industry observers note that among healthy participants, ultrasound stimulation improved heart rate variability, a measure of the natural differences in time between consecutive heartbeats. This measurement provides insight into how the body's nervous system responds to stress and adjusts to changing conditions.

Industry observers note that brain imaging revealed changes in neural circuits involved in emotional processing. Together, these findings suggest that improving REM sleep through targeted stimulation could potentially support emotional regulation and the ability to cope with stress.

"REM sleep is not just about dreaming -- it's about emotional reset and stress adaptation," explained Gregory Fonzo, assistant professor in the Dell Medical School's Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and one of the project's co-PIs. "By enhancing REM, we may help people better cope with stress and improve their overall well-being.".

These possibilities are especially interesting because REM sleep disturbances have been linked to depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Current approaches to sleep problems often involve medication or behavioral therapy. Although these treatments can be effective, medications may produce unwanted side effects, and existing approaches do not always directly address the biological processes responsible for disrupted REM sleep.

It has been revealed that A device capable of influencing those processes without drugs or surgery could therefore offer an additional treatment option. However, the researchers have not yet established whether NEUSLeeP can improve symptoms of mental health disorders.

A New Direction for Treating Insomnia and PTSD.

Building on the initial findings, the research team plans to conduct larger clinical trials to confirm the patch's effects and investigate its potential use in people with PTSD, depression, and chronic insomnia.

Beyond treating sleep disorders, the technology could eventually support sleep monitoring at home and provide scientists with a latest way to study how deep brain regions influence sleep. Researchers also envision personalized therapies that could be adjusted to individual sleep patterns and needs.

Sources indicate that "Our vision is a future where patients with mental health disorders can optimize their sleep with a noninvasive and safe treatment," said Vincent Mysliwiec, M.D., a professor at UT Health San Antonio, a leading expert in sleep disorders, and another co-PI on the project. "This technology could help millions of people get the restorative sleep they need.".

The team is already taking steps toward making NEUSLeeP available beyond the research setting. Working with the university's commercialization unit, Discovery to Impact, the researchers are exploring how to bring the device to market and have filed a patent application covering the technology.

If future studies confirm the early results, this wearable ultrasound patch could become a valuable upcoming tool for improving REM sleep and potentially addressing conditions associated with poor sleep.

In a recent development, other members of the research team include William D. Moscoso-Barrera, Mengxia Yu, Mengmeng Yao, Jinmo Jeong, Ilya Pyatnitskiy, Anakaren Romero Lozano, Jiachen Wang, Ju-Chun Hsieh, Tony Sungjin Chae, Daniel Song, Julieta Garcia, Rithvik Mittapalli, and Adam Bush of the Department of Biomedical Engineering; Benjamin Baird of the College of Natural Sciences' Department of Psychology; and Wynn Legon of Virginia Tech's Fralin Biomedical Research Institute.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1737 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Realtor ↗ Open Full Page

The Rise of the House Manager: Why Busy Families Are Outsourcing Everyday Tasks

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Between managing the demands of work and keeping up with everything at home, it can feel like there are never enough hours in the day.
  • For busy, overscheduled families, hiring a house manager may be the key to reclaiming valuable time, reducing daily stress, and bringing a little more balance to everyday life.
  • For those who are unfamiliar with this trending form of home support, a house manager is basically someone who keeps track of things behind the scenes so you can off-load some of your never-ending to-do list.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Between managing the demands of work and keeping up with everything at home, it can feel like there are never enough hours in the day.

For busy, overscheduled families, hiring a house manager may be the key to reclaiming valuable time, reducing daily stress, and bringing a little more balance to everyday life.

For those who are unfamiliar with this trending form of home support, a house manager is basically someone who keeps track of things behind the scenes so you can off-load some of your never-ending to-do list.

Sources indicate that "A house manager takes on the parts of the household a family chooses to hand off—that means both the everyday work and the planning behind it, from start to finish," notes Kelly Hubbell, founder and CEO of Sage Haus, a thriving house manager placement organization. "Think meals, laundry, errands, calendars, pet care, and home projects. A house manager doesn't just complete tasks ... they anticipate what's needed and handle it without being asked.".

In other words, a house manager is an added support system that helps keep a household functioning efficiently.

The simplest definition of a house manger is someone who helps facilitate everyday life behind the scenes.

"A housekeeper cleans, a nanny cares for the kids, a house manager owns whole areas of the household, from planning to follow-through," claims Hubbell.

Recent findings suggest that there can be overlap. A house manager might tidy, do laundry, or prepare meals, depending on what the family hands off. The difference is ownership.

It has been revealed that "Take laundry: A housekeeper might wash what's in the basket, whereas a house manager who owns laundry knows the soccer uniform has to be clean by Saturday, without a reminder," explains Hubbell. "The work that's different is the thinking behind the household.".

The best house managers have sharp judgment and the ability to strategy ahead, juggle several schedules and tasks at once, manage vendors, and make good decisions within the scope a family has agreed to, according to Hubbell.

They're proactive and notice what needs attention before anyone asks. And because they're in someone's home, trust, reliability, and discretion are essential.

Industry observers note that "People come to it from lots of backgrounds: nannies whose kids aged out of needing a nanny, teachers, hospitality and operations managers, military spouses who have set up a household in four cities, and moms coming back into the workforce after years of running their own homes—frankly, the hardest training there is," claims Hubbell, whose network now includes over 7,000 house managers in the U.S. and Canada, though Sage Haus accepts only about 5% of applicants to ensure quality.

"As AI changes the jobs available, this work depends on what technology can't supply: human judgment, trust, and care," she explains.

Basically, house managers are gaining traction because people are burning out, especially women.

"Most families hit a point where their life, career, or ambitions can't grow any further without more support—I call that the support ceiling," states Hubbell. "They don't need to scale back their dreams. They need to scale up their support.".

Industry observers note that many families already have some help, like a cleaner every other week, a nanny/sitter, or groceries on autopilot. But someone still has to hold it all together—the noticing, planning, and following up.

"That's the mental load, and research shows it usually stays with mom, even as her career and earnings grow," says Hubbell.

It has been revealed that according to a 2024 study from the University of Bath and the University of Melbourne, mothers in the U.S. carry 71% of mental-load tasks, and while women’s employment and earnings reduce their physical household labor, it does not shrink their cognitive burden.

It has been revealed that "Real estate has always recognized the value of a well-maintained home. What we're only beginning to recognize is the value of the work required to maintain it," states Laura Marie Rivera, a gender equity and unpaid labor researcher and host of the "Motherhood Advantage" podcast. "The rise of professional house managers puts a job title and salary on responsibilities that mothers have managed for generations—largely without either.".

Unpaid household work in the U.S. is worth up to $6 trillion a year, and none of it shows up in the GDP. However, the rise of house mangers is finally putting a dollar amount on the mental load of keeping a home operational.

Industry observers note that "Paying someone to manage a household doesn't just reveal the economic value of the work, it reveals the scope of the work," notes Rivera. "We're not witnessing the invention of a new profession so much as the professional recognition of work that has been hiding in plain sight.".

The good news is that having a house manager isn't only for the wealthy. In general, cost depends on where you live and what you need the house manager to take on.

It has been revealed that "Families hire and pay house managers directly, and pay ranges from $25 to more than $50 an hour depending on location and scope," notes Hubbell. "It doesn't have to be full time: 80% of families start with part-time help, averaging 15 to 20 hours per week.".

Industry observers note that for many families, a house manager can be a more practical investment than several separate kinds of help, because it brings that support together in one role. However, there are still options when budgetary constraints prohibit the employment of a house manager.

Sources indicate that "Support doesn't have to start with a hire," states Hubbell. "It can begin with mapping out everything it takes to run your home and deciding what to drop, what to share with a partner, and where you need help most.".

That being said, for those who can swing it, having a house manager can be life-changing.

In theory this all sounds amazing, but what's it like in practice? We checked in with a house manager and a family that's hired a house manager to get the inside scoop. But the short version is, both are very happy with their decision.

Before becoming a house manager, Terry Boch worked as an executive assistant, but also spent years as a stay-at-home mom raising her three children.

It has been revealed that once they were grown and she reentered the work force, she was enjoying being an executive assistant again but realized she wanted something less computer-focused and more hands-on. That's when she came across a job post seeking house managers. Intrigued, she pursued the opportunity, was matched with a family in Upcoming Jersey, and found it was a perfect fit for her skill set.

"I love transforming an already beautiful house into a warm, welcoming home that looks and smells inviting every day," notes Boch, whose primary responsibilities include meal planning, grocery shopping and meal preparation, laundry, resetting bedrooms and living spaces, and plant care. "I work approximately 15–20 hours per week, but I like to say that I get to play house in a home I could never afford.".

In reality, however, Boch says she sees what she does as much more about creating a home than maintaining a house.

According to recent reports, "Although my interaction with the children is limited, knowing that I can contribute to an environment where they feel comfortable, cared for, and happy brings me tremendous joy," says Boch. "I love making a home feel welcoming, anticipating what a family needs, and taking pride in all the little things that make everyday life more enjoyable. I'm not a house cleaner; I'm a homemaker at heart.".

On the flip side, Krissel Varela found her way to the idea of hiring a house manager online.

It has been revealed that "Following Sage Haus on social media really opened my eyes to what household support could look like," notes Varela. "I had always thought about help in a more traditional sense, like a nanny or someone full-time, but started realizing we could shape the support around what our family actually needed.".

Though she'd had a nanny when her kids were younger and she was working a corporate job, once they reached school age, they didn't need that kind of assistance anymore. However, their lives didn't get less busy.

Recent findings suggest that "Between school, sports, activities, keeping our household running, and now building a business of my own, there are just so many moving pieces," says Varela. The idea of a house manager made sense for her family, though they didn't need someone full time.

Sources indicate that "Right now, we have help about 8 to 10 hours a week, and even though that's not a huge number of hours, the impact feels so much bigger," indicates Varela. Her house manager is usually with them on Mondays and Thursdays, with some flexibility predicated on their needs.

"Between laundry, household organization, errands, and all those little tasks that add up throughout the week, having someone share those responsibilities makes such a difference," she adds.

Though it's been only a few months, Varela says she can already feel a huge life shift.

According to recent reports, "It's not just the actual hours saved; it's also the mental space that comes from knowing someone else is helping keep things moving without having to manage every little detail," says Varela. "It's also given me more room for the things that are easy to push aside when life gets busy, whether that's spending quality time with my husband, enjoying our weekends, or even having a little time for myself. Having that extra support has really helped me be more intentional about where my time and energy go.".

And that is exactly what a house manager is supposed to do, open up space for life at home to be about more than just getting by every day.

In a recent development, "People should also know there's a cost to getting support and a cost to going without it, whether that's your health, your relationships, or your connection with your family," says Hubbell. "The goal isn't to outsource your life; it's to get enough support to be present for it.".

Kimberly Dawn Neumann is a journalist based in Newly introduced York City and the author of hundreds of articles on home-related topics for major publications, including Forbes, Real Simple, and Realtor.com. For more information, visit www.KDNeumann.com or IG @dancerscribe.

#122074. Breaking: Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1500 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1500 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A massive study involving more than 340,000 adults has uncovered a surprising difference in the health risks associated with wine, beer, cider, and spirits.
  • It has been revealed that researchers found that low to moderate wine consumption was associated with a lower risk of death, particularly from cardiovascular disease.
  • The results also reinforce a broader conclusion from previous research: drinking less alcohol is generally better for health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A massive study involving more than 340,000 adults has uncovered a surprising difference in the health risks associated with wine, beer, cider, and spirits. Although heavy drinking was linked to worse health outcomes regardless of the beverage, the picture was more complicated among people who consumed smaller amounts of alcohol.

It has been revealed that researchers found that low to moderate wine consumption was associated with a lower risk of death, particularly from cardiovascular disease. In contrast, similar amounts of beer, cider, and spirits were linked to a higher risk. The findings, presented at the American College of Cardiology's Annual Scientific Session (ACC.26), suggest that both the type and quantity of alcohol may influence its relationship with long-term health.

The results also reinforce a broader conclusion from previous research: drinking less alcohol is generally better for health. Importantly, the upcoming findings do not establish that wine itself protects against disease.

"These results come from the general population, and in certain high-risk groups, such as people with chronic diseases or cardiovascular conditions, the risks could be even higher," stated Zhangling Chen, MD, PhD, a professor at the Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University in China and the study's senior author.

How a Study of 340,000 Adults Measured Alcohol Risk.

To investigate the relationship between drinking habits and longevity, scientists examined data from 340,924 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank between 2006 and 2022. The UK Biobank is a large research resource that collects health and lifestyle information to help scientists investigate factors associated with disease and mortality.

According to recent reports, participants reported their alcohol consumption through dietary questionnaires when they joined the study. Researchers then classified them into four groups based on how much pure alcohol they typically consumed each day or week, rather than simply counting drinks.

According to recent reports, this distinction matters because beer, wine, and spirits contain different concentrations of alcohol. For comparison, a 12-ounce can of beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, and a 1.5-ounce shot of spirits each provide approximately 14 grams of pure alcohol.

In a recent development, people consuming fewer than 20 g (about 1.5 standard drinks) per week were placed in the never or occasional drinking group. Low consumption was defined as 20 g per week up to 20 g per day for men, and 20 g per week up to 10 g per day for women.

Moderate drinking was defined as 20 g to 40 g (about 1.5 to three standard drinks) daily for men and 10 g to 20 g daily for women. High consumption meant more than 40 g (about three drinks) per day for men or more than 20 g (about 1.5 drinks) per day for women.

Researchers followed participants' health outcomes for an average of more than 13 years, allowing them to examine how drinking patterns were associated with deaths from different causes.

Wine, Beer, and Spirits Show Different Heart Health Risks.

Recent findings suggest that the clearest finding concerned heavy alcohol consumption. Compared with people who never drank or consumed alcohol only occasionally, heavy drinkers had a 24% higher risk of dying from any cause. Their risk of dying from cancer was 36% higher, while their risk of dying from heart disease was 14% higher.

These increased risks were associated with heavy drinking regardless of whether participants preferred wine, beer, cider, or spirits.

Sources indicate that however, the results became more surprising when researchers examined low and moderate alcohol consumption. At these levels, the type of beverage was associated with substantially different outcomes.

People who consumed wine in low to moderate amounts had a significantly lower risk of death, while those who consumed comparable amounts of beer, cider, or spirits had a significantly higher risk.

The contrast was especially striking for cardiovascular disease, a broad category of conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels. Moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease than people who never or only occasionally drank alcohol.

By comparison, even low consumption of beer, cider, or spirits was associated with a 9% higher risk of cardiovascular death.

In a recent development, these percentages describe relative differences in risk between groups, not the absolute probability that an individual will die from cardiovascular disease. Because the research was observational, the findings also cannot demonstrate that choosing one alcoholic beverage over another directly changes a person's risk.

In a recent development, "Our findings help clarify previously mixed evidence on low to moderate alcohol consumption," Chen remarked. "These findings can help refine guidance, emphasizing that the health risks of alcohol depend not only on the amount of alcohol consumed, but also on the type of beverage. Even low to moderate intake of spirits, beer, or cider is linked to higher mortality, while low to moderate intake of wine may carry lower risk.".

Why Might Wine Be Linked to Lower Heart Risks?

Researchers identified several possible explanations for the differences, including the chemical composition of wine and the habits of people who drink it.

Red wine contains polyphenols, naturally occurring compounds found in plants that can have antioxidant properties. Antioxidants help counter certain chemical reactions involving unstable molecules that can damage cells. Some polyphenols have been investigated for potential benefits to blood vessels and cardiovascular function.

These compounds could contribute to the associations observed in wine drinkers, although the study did not establish that they were responsible for the lower mortality risk.

Another possible explanation involves how and when people drink.

According to recent reports, wine is more commonly consumed alongside meals, and wine drinkers often report healthier diets and lifestyle habits. Drinking wine may therefore be associated with other behaviors that support cardiovascular health.

Beer, cider, and spirits, on the other hand, are more frequently consumed outside of meals. In this study, people who favored these beverages also tended to have poorer overall diet quality and other lifestyle factors associated with increased health risks.

Such differences make it difficult to separate the effects of the alcohol itself from the characteristics and habits of the people consuming it.

"Taken together, these factors suggest that the type of alcohol, how it is consumed, and the associated lifestyle behaviors all contribute to the observed differences in mortality risk," Chen stated.

What the Findings Mean for Alcohol and Health.

To make their comparisons more reliable, the researchers statistically adjusted their analyses for numerous factors that might influence mortality. These included age and other demographic characteristics, socioeconomic circumstances, lifestyle behaviors, and cardiometabolic health.

Sources indicate that cardiometabolic factors include conditions and measurements related to heart and metabolic health, such as blood pressure, blood sugar regulation, and cholesterol levels. The analyses also accounted for family histories of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

Even with these adjustments, the researchers emphasized several notable limitations.

Because the study was observational, it could identify associations between alcohol consumption and mortality but could not prove that particular beverages caused better or worse outcomes. Other differences between participants may have influenced the findings despite the statistical adjustments.

Alcohol intake was also measured through questionnaires completed when participants first entered the study. That information depended on participants accurately reporting their own drinking habits, and it did not capture changes in consumption during the years that followed.

Industry observers note that another consideration is that UK Biobank participants tend to be healthier than the general population. This could limit how well the findings apply to other groups of people.

In a recent development, the researchers suggested that high-quality randomized trials could provide stronger evidence about the health effects of different drinking patterns. Such studies would help clarify whether the observed differences reflect the beverages themselves or other factors associated with their consumption.

Nevertheless, the enormous study population and more than 13 years of average follow-up provide considerable statistical strength. By examining specific types of alcohol, different levels of consumption, and multiple causes of death, the research offers a more detailed picture of alcohol's potential health risks than many earlier investigations.

The findings highlight an notable distinction: while heavy drinking is consistently associated with harmful health outcomes, the relationships observed at lower consumption levels may depend on beverage choice, drinking habits, and broader lifestyle patterns.

For now, the apparent advantage among wine drinkers should not be interpreted as a reason to start drinking wine for heart health. The evidence points to a complex relationship between alcohol and mortality, rather than proving that any alcoholic drink offers protection.

Ziyue Li presented the study, "Alcohol Use at Mid-Life and All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality," at ACC.26.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:41 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Google LLC today released a new version of Gemini’s Mac client that can interact with other apps on the user’s computer.

The feature is available in the U.S. on launch. It requires a Google AI subscription, which equips consumer Google accounts with a broader lineup of artificial intelligence tools. The offering also includes additional storage space and certain other features.

Industry observers note that people can instruct Gemini to launch a local app by including the command “@Computer use” in their prompts. For example, a designer could upload a sketch of a vehicle and ask the AI assistant to turn it into a three-dimensional animation. Gemini finds the local app that is needed for the task, creates a project blueprint and carries out the work step by step.

In a recent development, the assistant supports tasks that comprise dozens of actions. Furthermore, consumers can use the output of a newly completed Gemini workflow to launch follow-up projects. A user could have the assistant generate a visual asset in a design tool and then turn it into a mini-app with Visual Studio Code.

Industry observers note that gemini can interact with not only local apps but also web services. That means it can load data from webpages into programs that run on the user’s machine, as well as move data in the opposite direction and between cloud services.

The AI carries out its work in a background window. As a result, people don’t have to pause their work while the assistant is running. They can track Gemini workflows via a preview pane built into the Mac client’s chat window. Additionally, Google has included controls that make it possible to give Gemini feedback mid-task.

“Privacy and safety are built in: you choose which apps Gemini can access, watch every step live, pause at any time, and approve key actions before they happen,” Michael Friedman, Google’s group product manager for the Gemini app, wrote in a blog post.

The Mac version of Muse, Meta Platforms Inc.’s recently released AI agent, can also interact with local apps and data. Furthermore, a cloud-based virtual machine enables it to perform tasks even when the user’s computer is offline. Dots, a competing service from OpenAI Group PBC, offers a similar capability.

Google may seek to match its rivals’ cloud-based workflow hosting features in the future. The tech giant can also extend Gemini in other ways. Notably, it could bring Gemini’s computer use mode to additional operating systems and add features for business users. OpenAI’s Dots already includes capabilities designed to automate business workflows such as procurement.
