📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:34 amNovember 17, 2026 at 8:37 am.
  • Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007, “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list.
  • The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:34 amNovember 17, 2026 at 8:37 am.

Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007, “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list.

The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.

“Since technology by itself can’t fix a broken system, we’re rebuilding the whole system to make it work for you — combining a software firm, a group of doctors and nurses, and an insurance company,” reads the introductory message on the site.

His co-founder is Dr. Connie Chen, an internist who co-founded digital health company Vida Health and spent more than seven years at mental health benefits company Lyra Health, first as chief medical officer and then as chief operating officer, as Lyra grew to a $5.6 billion valuation.

Recent findings suggest that this is not a modest app for booking doctor’s appointments. Under the corporate name Silica Health Inc., the company filed a trademark application last month covering health maintenance organization services — HMOs are health looks that pair insurance coverage with their own networks of doctors — along with insurance administration, medical billing and claims management.

Kelman, who is rarely at a loss for words, confirmed in response to our inquiry that he wasn’t ready to talk yet. He wrote in a GeekWire guest column this month that he and his business partner would announce their plans “after we’ve built our product.”.

In a recent development, but after he posted about his team on LinkedIn last week, we got curious and couldn’t help but look around. Their resumes were a tip-off: In addition to Chen, the team includes an engineer who spent nearly seven years at tech-driven health insurer Oscar Health.

According to recent reports, searching Kelman’s name in state business licenses turned up Silica Health, with Kelman and Chen listed as officers. Plugging that name into the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office’s database produced exactly one result: the application for “Sojourn Health.”.

From there, it was a short trip to sojournhealth.com, which sketches out the plan.

Why health care: Kelman spent 20 years running Redfin, which stood out in the real estate industry for employing its agents rather than treating them as independent contractors. That turns out to be part of the origin story.

Industry observers note that “Almost every year after its IPO, Redfin had to re-consider whether to keep employing its own agents, because of their rising healthcare costs,” Sojourn’s founders page explains. The options were to make agents contractors, ask employees to pay more, or cover less care.

“The choices were all terrible,” it states.

Chen’s bio on the site describes a career spent on one problem: how employers can give their employees better care at lower cost.

As a primary-care doctor, she saw her patients’ health and finances rise and fall together, the site states, and concluded that “a system taped together from broken parts couldn’t serve either.”.

Kelman, by his own account, is upcoming to the field. In his guest column, he wrote that when he thought about the companies he would have been proud to start, they were all in one particular industry. He didn’t say which one, but it’s not hard to guess now.

“I had no experience in that industry, but a friend mentioned I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing,” he wrote.

The team: In a LinkedIn post last week, Kelman stated the founding team also includes Jennifer Chao and Ben Baker, with Sasha Aickin “adding some part-time magic.” He promised that “the mission is good and the ambition is vast.”.

The lineup draws on Kelman’s past and the health insurance world:.

Recent findings suggest that chao and Aickin both worked with Kelman at Plumtree Software, the enterprise software tech giant he co-founded in 1996, before following him to Redfin. Sojourn’s recruiting page nods to the pattern: “We’re honored by the old friends who have worked with us from company to company, but we’re also eager to bring in upcoming blood.”.

The Sojourn site claims the organization is likely to have engineering hubs in Seattle for the member experience, San Francisco for the clinical platform, and Austin for the claims system.

AI all the way down: Sojourn is hiring software engineers and product managers “at every level of the organization.” The first thing on its list of qualifications: experience using frontier AI tools “to generate reliable, high-scale production code.”.

That fits with his guest column. A recruiter told him Seattle’s startup scene was “dead,” he wrote, and a friend described CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at companies with old code. Kelman wrote that “the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.”.

What we don’t know: The website doesn’t say when Sojourn plans to launch or where it will offer coverage first, although Chen’s bio suggests employers will be key customers, describing a care model “designed around the member and the employer who pays for it.”.

Sources indicate that A new health strategy typically requires state insurance licenses and significant capital reserves, and the organization hasn’t disclosed any funding. Kelman wrote in his column that he “met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea,” but he didn’t name them, and a search of SEC filings for Sojourn Health and Silica Health found no record of a fundraise.

In June, he joined venture firm Greylock as an executive in residence, saying at the time that he was still looking to start a fresh mission-driven enterprise, a process that involved “exploring ideas that are never going to work and howling at the moon.” It’s not clear whether Greylock is among his backers.

Kelman stepped down as Redfin CEO in January, six months after Rocket Companies completed its $1.75 billion acquisition of the Seattle brokerage. He remarked at the time that he wanted to find “another mission-driven enterprise outside of real estate.”.

Industry observers note that he appears to have found one. Whether health care is more or less screwed up than real estate is a question that will have to wait until he’s ready to chat.

Howard Hanna sued over $395 real estate transaction fee

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Howard Hanna Real Estate Services is joining the growing roster of real estate firms facing a lawsuit over a “transaction fee” a consumer was allegedly forced to pay in conjunction with their real estate transaction.
  • Earlier this month, first-time homebuyer Dena Bergamasco filed a suit against Howard Hanna over a $395 “Realtor Transaction Fee” she claims she was charged on top of the buyer broker commission she paid related to her October 2021 home purchase.
  • Bergamasco is being represented by Kopelowitz Ostrow P.A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Howard Hanna Real Estate Services is joining the growing roster of real estate firms facing a lawsuit over a “transaction fee” a consumer was allegedly forced to pay in conjunction with their real estate transaction.

Earlier this month, first-time homebuyer Dena Bergamasco filed a suit against Howard Hanna over a $395 “Realtor Transaction Fee” she claims she was charged on top of the buyer broker commission she paid related to her October 2021 home purchase.

Bergamasco is being represented by Kopelowitz Ostrow P.A. one of the firms representing plaintiff Gregory Deivert in his transaction fee lawsuit filed against a Keller Williams franchise last month.

Attorneys for Bergamasco claim in the filing that as her buyer broker Howard Hanna breached its fiduciary duty and violated the state’s Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law in charging her this fee, which the suit describes as a “cash grab.”.

Bargamasco claims that the $395 fee was charged “for nothing” with “no service behind it, no cost behind it, and no name that accurately describes it.”.

“It is money taken from a client by the broker who was supposed to be looking out for her,” the complaint states.

Recent findings suggest that according to the complaint, the fee was “wedged”  between third-party charges for a pest inspection fee and an owner’s title insurance premium in the closing disclosure. Additionally, the complaint alleges that the brokerage coaches agents to tell clients that the fee is mandatory and serves a “processing” or “administrative” purpose.

Industry observers note that in the filing, Bergamasco’s attorneys state that she paid $217,000 for her home, with $213,069 of this coming from a federally insured mortgage and $10,850 coming from a second loan from the Pennsylvania Housing Finance Agency. In addition to this, the sellers awarded her a $7,300 credit to use toward closing costs. In total, the filing states that Bergamasco brought $788.95 in cash to her closing, not even double the cost of the alleged fee. According to the filing, with the home purchase transaction occurring prior to the Sitzer/Burnett commission lawsuit settlement, the plaintiff’s buyer broker commission was paid by the home seller and that Bergamasco paid for the paperwork completed by the settlement agent and title insurance provider at the closing.

In a recent development, the suit is seeking class action status and the plaintiff has demanded a jury trial. Bergamasco noted she is seeking damages and a permanent injunction preventing Howard Hanna from charging this fee in the future.

Howard Hanna did not immediately return HousingWire’s request for comment regarding the lawsuit.

The complaint claims that the practice of charging consumers a “transaction fee” is not unique to Howard Hanna. This is evidenced in the other lawsuits that have popped up this year, including the lawsuit against Keller Williams Elite over an alleged $650 “broker fee” and a since voluntarily dismissed lawsuit filed against Compass over an alleged $475 transaction fee.

Some reports, such as one from the Consumer Policy Center, claim that consumers pay up to $2 billion in brokerage transaction fees each year.

Hopefully, bulls pick up the rally, though for now the momentum is slow. The descending volume on the price upside suggests fading. The divergence of moving averages is an anti-volatility signal right now rather than anything else. All of them still sit above the price, with the nearest one around $1.13.

It mostly followed the general uptrend but tumbled swiftly due to the general reversal of the cryptocurrency market.

In a recent development, the worrying part is, ironically, the recovery of RSI, which is slowly moving above the oversold zone and opens up the way for an additional leg down. RSI is around 33 now, up from its low near 27.

It has been revealed that the matter is the historic pattern XRP is forming: a constant downtrend with occasional recoveries that quickly turn into new breakdowns. In early November, XRP bounced from around $1.20 to the $1.30 area. The breakdown that followed took the price down by around 30% in under two weeks.

Recent findings suggest that the downtrend is way stronger than the bullish reversal attempts XRP had earlier this month. Unfortunately, it can create a sustainable downtrend that can last for months, and considering XRP's price of $0.99, this is not something investors want.

The market is weak, and it might get weaker. The confirmation of a market recovery would only come if we witness specific signs of a bull run: higher highs and sustained buying.

Early data points to Vulcan’s first stage in launch failure that cost Amazon 40 Leo satellites

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (603 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:52 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am.
  • 18: ULA said Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance.
  • Early data suggests the first stage of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket underperformed just after liftoff Sunday, leaving it unable to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit, ULA noted Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:52 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am.

Update, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA said Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Early data suggests the first stage of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket underperformed just after liftoff Sunday, leaving it unable to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit, ULA noted Tuesday.

It has been revealed that in its first detailed account of the failure, ULA cited “low booster performance,” using its term for Vulcan’s core first stage. As a result, the stage separated when the rocket was too low and moving too slowly to reach orbit.

Sources indicate that that stage is powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. However, ULA didn’t say what caused the shortfall or whether the engines played a role. ULA noted it’s very early in the process and that it wants to avoid speculation until the investigation is complete.

Recent findings suggest that the Centaur upper stage appears to have started normally, and its two L3Harris RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the shortfall, ULA said. The six solid rocket boosters made by Northrop Grumman, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally.

The Federal Aviation Administration will oversee the ULA-led investigation and approve its final report, including any fixes.

What changed since Sunday: ULA’s account changes the picture from Sunday, when the failure appeared to come about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn.

According to recent reports, ULA stated Tuesday that it appears to have lost telemetry and the mission at about that point, but that the trouble began just after liftoff. Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned before separating.

Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp, asked on X why the Kent, Wash.-based tech giant hadn’t commented, replied Tuesday morning.

“It is ULA’s mission so they should provide the updates,” Limp wrote. “We are supporting them with data and analysis from the BE-4s. Team Blue continues to ready the pad and Newly introduced Glenn for our return to flight.”.

It has been revealed that impact on Amazon Leo: Sunday’s launch was the first of 38 Vulcan missions Amazon bought for its planned rival to SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

It has been revealed that amazon also has 24 launches reserved on Upcoming Glenn, which uses seven BE-4s on its first stage. New Glenn has been grounded since an oxygen valve problem caused one to explode during a ground test in May. Blue Origin retrofitted the BE-4s on Sunday’s Vulcan with a fix for that problem, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight.

Before Sunday, Amazon had rolled out 396 satellites for its Redmond-based Leo program on 14 successful missions since April 2025, most recently on an Atlas 5 in July. The Federal Communications Commission let Amazon keep deploying satellites after it fell short of a July 30 deadline to have 1,616 in service. Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy all 3,232 of its first-generation satellites.

Amazon has noted it plans to start commercial internet service this year through Leo, formerly known as Project Kuiper. The next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

Homebuilders’ $30B buying spree has cooled; now it’s all execution

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2839 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the better part of 15 years, U.S.
  • In a recent development, the buying continued through 2026, with Berkshire Hathaway‘s $8.5 billion acquisition of Taylor Morrison and Sumitomo Forestry‘s approximately $4.5 billion purchase of Tri Pointe Homes among the year’s largest deals.
  • It has been revealed that yet even as those transactions have reshaped the industry’s competitive landscape, the economics of homebuilding have shifted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the better part of 15 years, U.S. homebuilding has been on a mergers-and-acquisitions buying spree. Since 2010, more than 200 homebuilder transactions have conservatively totaled more than $30 billion in announced deal value, based on just seven of the largest acquisitions and excluding scores of private-tech giant transactions whose purchase prices were never disclosed.

In a recent development, the buying continued through 2026, with Berkshire Hathaway‘s $8.5 billion acquisition of Taylor Morrison and Sumitomo Forestry‘s approximately $4.5 billion purchase of Tri Pointe Homes among the year’s largest deals. More recent transactions included Daiwa House subsidiary Stanley Martin‘s July acquisition of Holiday Builders, Dream Finders Homes‘ August acquisition of Beazer Homes, and Century Communities’ October purchase of HistoryMaker Homes.

It has been revealed that yet even as those transactions have reshaped the industry’s competitive landscape, the economics of homebuilding have shifted. Weak demand, costly sales incentives, shrinking margins, and uncertainty over land and home values are forcing acquirers to reconsider not only which businesses are worth buying but also how the companies they already own should operate.

“We’re not busy now,” one deeply experienced homebuilding M&A dealmaker told me recently. “This is no time to be trying to take a seller to market for acquisition. Nothing’s happening.”.

That assessment does not mean homebuilding consolidation has ended. It’s still “morning time in America” for homebuilding’s inevitable grind toward concentration of fewer, ever larger, more industrialized homebuilding giants.

My source’s observation suggests that the economics of bringing upcoming sellers to market have become harder, even as the largest and best-capitalized acquirers continue pursuing strategic combinations.

Business and investment models in homebuilding can look remarkably good when demand, prices, and asset values are rising. The real test comes when the cycle turns, gravity takes hold, and assumptions that worked on the way up begin to break down. That’s when the industry’s outliers distinguish themselves, not simply through stronger balance sheets, but by how well their people work together, how rapidly they adapt their processes, how effectively they serve customers, and how consistently they outperform competitors when business conditions get messy.

It has been revealed that that is the test now confronting the companies assembled through homebuilding’s extraordinary consolidation era. Have their acquisitions produced merely bigger enterprises, or have they developed the leadership, operating discipline, local knowledge, and capacity to improve that will make them fundamentally better homebuilders with greater connectivity to and attainability for America’s economically bifurcated households?

The answer will increasingly depend on what happens inside the enterprises they’ve acquired. The challenge is to capture the value of their land positions while developing the people, operating systems, technologies, and organizational capabilities needed to replenish those positions, improve profitability, and serve customers more efficiently in a difficult market likely to extend into 2027 and potentially 2028.

That is where the next, and perhaps most demanding, phase of homebuilding consolidation begins.

Homebuilding acquisitions are distinct from many other corporate combinations because the value of the acquired business is inseparable from its land positions and the people capable of turning those positions – sustainably and repeatedly – into profitable homes.

In a recent development, an attractive acquisition may bring years of controlled lots, entitled development opportunities, established relationships with landowners and municipalities, and access to markets that would take an outsider years to enter. It may also include an experienced management team, trusted trade relationships, established brands and the organizational knowledge and local intel needed to perpetuate the business beyond its current land pipeline.

Those assets are related, but they are not interchangeable. When one goes missing, the others quickly fall out of balance. The value of the land depends on its location, basis, development requirements, timing, and the demand for homes that can be built on it profitably. Realizing that value depends on decisions about product, construction costs, sales strategy, purchasing, development sequencing, and capital allocation.

An acquirer that buys a good land portfolio but loses the ability to develop and replenish it efficiently may find that the acquisition’s original promise was a mere blip. An acquirer that preserves an admired local management organization without improving its operating economics may find that the business remains well regarded yet increasingly uncompetitive.

Industry observers note that successful acquisitions require balancing those two realities. The objective is to capture the value of the acquired land and operating platform as a launching pad for building the leadership, relationships, systems, and financial discipline needed to extend that profitability long after the original inventory has been delivered.

That balance of 100% binding capabilities becomes harder to hold together when market conditions weaken.

For years, one of the most attractive features of selling to Berkshire Hathaway’s Clayton Properties Group or one of the major Japan-based acquirers was the prospect of continuity.

Sources indicate that many regional builders joined larger, well-capitalized ownership organizations while retaining key elements of their identities, management teams, local relationships, and operating independence. That approach appealed to owners seeking liquidity or a succession solution without losing the character of the companies they had built.

Sources indicate that it also made strategic sense. Local knowledge, land relationships, management experience, customer trust, and an almost irreplicable entrepreneurial fire and come-what-may resiliency were among the assets the buyers sought to acquire.

But serving as a benevolent, deep-pocketed, and patient capital-access channel for a local autonomy confederation across an expanding collection of businesses comes at a cost. Separate purchasing organizations, technology systems, back-office functions, product-development practices, and management structures can limit the benefits of larger ownership. When sales are strong and margins are healthy, those costs may be easier to absorb. When sales slow, incentives rise, and profitability contracts, the economics become less forgiving.

According to recent reports, the pressure to coordinate operations, consolidate functions, standardize selected processes, and reduce unnecessary overhead intensifies. So do difficult decisions about regional leadership, divisional responsibilities, and the roles of managers at the divisional and neighborhood level who helped make the acquired businesses successful in the first place.

Industry observers note that those decisions can be disruptive, especially for employees and former owners who believed their companies would continue operating as they had before the acquisition and, in some cases, had enjoyed a solid few-year runway of exactly that. Some will regard the changes as evidence that the fresh parent does not understand the business it acquired. Others will see them as necessary steps toward strengthening the combined organization.

Industry observers note that eliminating management positions or consolidating administrative functions does not, by itself, demonstrate operational improvement. Nor does a departure from established practices necessarily indicate that an acquirer has made a strategic mistake or an unforced error.

The relevant test is whether the changes improve the organization’s ability to develop land, build homes, serve customers, maintain valuable relationships and generate returns that stakeholders and owners can count on as durable. That is a more useful standard than judging an acquisition by how many legacy executives remain in place or by how many familiar operating practices survive.

Recent findings suggest that an key distinction exists among the companies driving the latest phase of consolidation. Daiwa House, Sekisui House, Sumitomo Forestry, and Berkshire Hathaway operate with strategic planning horizons and ownership structures that can offer greater flexibility than the quarter-to-quarter performance pressures faced by many publicly traded U.S. homebuilders.

Industry observers note that the Japanese companies are publicly traded, and Berkshire Hathaway is accountable to its shareholders. None is insulated from financial performance requirements. But their diversified businesses, substantial resources, and long-term commitments to housing and related industries can allow them to invest in capabilities whose returns may take years to materialize.

So far, that difference has played out as an “acquirer-of-choice” factor as homebuilding firm sellers considered how firms organize and develop the businesses they acquire.

Recent findings suggest that A longer-term ownership philosophy does not require codifying every management position or maintaining every regional operating structure indefinitely. In fact, patient capital may be most valuable when it enables an organization to undertake difficult transformations without expecting every investment to deliver an immediate earnings benefit.

The challenge is to distinguish costs that can be eliminated from capabilities that need strengthening.

Recent findings suggest that japan-based companies also have another potentially important advantage. Their experience with industrialized construction, standardized components, manufacturing systems, production engineering and deeply vertical integration extends well beyond what is typical of conventional American site-built homebuilding.

According to recent reports, clayton also brings experience in manufactured housing, factory-based production, and vertically integrated housing-related businesses. Its expanding site-built platform, particularly following the Taylor Morrison acquisition, creates opportunities to combine capabilities that have historically operated in unrelated realms of the residential construction business.

Industry observers note that none of this means that industrialized methods developed elsewhere can simply be transplanted into American site-built construction. Differences in building codes, product preferences, transportation, trade labor, land development, and construction practices remain unsolved obstacles.

The industry has not yet demonstrated that these capabilities can be deployed broadly enough to transform the economics of conventional site-built housing. Still, the long-term strategic opportunity is hard to refute.

A collection of independently operated regional builders can provide market presence, land access, local expertise and “trust capital.” A more coordinated enterprise may also provide the common systems, product architecture, production volumes, and organizational learning needed to adapt industrialized methods across multiple markets.

As ambitions go, that’s far bigger than reducing SG&A. It also raises a question that applies to every major acquirer: Which capabilities should remain local, which should be shared across the enterprise, and which should be fundamentally reengineered into the holistic, interoperable system modern homebuilding organizations seem to need?

It has been revealed that homebuilding has long featured an argument over whether privately held regional builders are inherently better businesses than their larger public competitors. The case for private builders emphasizes their closeness to customers, knowledge of local land markets, relationships with municipalities and trades, and the loyalty and committed engagement of talented employees who have worked together for years.

Those advantages are real in many companies. They can influence everything from land acquisition opportunities to construction execution and customer referrals. But private ownership does not guarantee those qualities, just as public or institutional ownership does not necessarily diminish them.

A privately held company can become inefficient, undercapitalized, or resistant to change. A large enterprise can cultivate strong local leadership, build trusted community relationships, and adopt operating practices that improve the customer experience.

The more useful distinction concerns the quality of the operating organization, a characteristic we’ve talked about as homebuilding’s “outlier” factor.

In a recent development, does it put decisions in the hands of people with the knowledge to make them? Does it give those people the resources, information, and accountability to perform effectively? Can it identify successful practices and extend their benefits beyond the division where they originated?

Sources indicate that answers to those questions reveal more than public or private ownership labels. They also help explain why the integration decisions now confronting the major consolidators are so difficult. An organization can destroy valuable local capabilities by centralizing too much. It can also waste substantial resources and miss opportunities to improve by centralizing too little.

In a recent development, integration is knowing the difference. Some acquirers are good integrators. That doesn’t mean people swept up in them, or spat out due to them, agree.

For decades, scale in homebuilding has largely meant more closings, more communities, more controlled lots, greater geographic reach, and increased purchasing power that leads to market-share advantages. Those advantages remain as a bulwark of near-flywheel-like value creation. Larger builders can spread fixed costs across more homes, negotiate favorable supplier arrangements, diversify market exposure, and access capital on terms that smaller competitors may struggle to match.

Still, everyone who’s done well in the business can attest that size alone does not explain why some organizations consistently outperform others.

According to recent reports, A more meaningful definition of scale includes an enterprise’s ability to combine capital, land, local knowledge, talent, technology, and relationships into an operating system that continuously improves performance. In that sense, homebuilding was AI before AI was cool because its best operators knew and practiced “recursive learning” as a core skill set.

That means acquiring land at bases that support acceptable returns under realistic demand assumptions. It also means developing products that customers value without unnecessary design, material, or construction complexity.

It means coordinating suppliers and trades to reduce delays, rework, and waste. It also means developing managers who can exercise sound judgment locally while drawing on the organization’s broader capabilities. It also means using information gathered across markets to make better decisions throughout the enterprise.

Recent findings suggest that A builder operating in 20 markets should have opportunities to learn from 20 distinct sets of customers, land conditions, construction challenges, and operating practices. But those opportunities yield little advantage if the information remains trapped within individual divisions or if the organization lacks the discipline to identify and transfer improvements.

Industry observers note that this is where AI-powered data systems and other technology capabilities could change the economics of scale. Better demand forecasting, more accurate construction scheduling, earlier detection of cost overruns, improved land underwriting, and more systematic comparisons of product performance could help organizations spot problems sooner and make decisions faster.

In a recent development, AI could help reveal patterns that managers would otherwise struggle to recognize in large volumes of operational data. It could also make institutional knowledge more accessible to those making daily decisions about land, purchasing, construction, and sales.

But value will not come from installing technology alone. Companies will need reliable data, consistent definitions, disciplined operating processes, and managers who can distinguish useful insights from misleading conclusions. They will also need to recognize that an approach that works in one market may be a fool’s errand in another.

Competitive advantage will belong to organizations that can repeatedly measure performance, understand what drives it, test improvements, and incorporate what they learn into their operating practices. That is how scale becomes a capability rather than merely a measurement of size.

The difficult market conditions facing builders through 2027, and potentially into 2028, will make these distinctions more apparent. Management teams will face pressure to reduce overhead, preserve liquidity, reassess land commitments, control construction costs, and improve returns on capital. Some will need to reorganize divisions, consolidate functions, or change leadership.

The companies that emerge stronger will not necessarily be the ones that make the deepest cuts. They will be the ones that understand which costs can be eliminated without harming the business and which investments are necessary to improve its future performance. That requires financial discipline, but it also requires patience, sound leadership judgment, and a willingness to challenge established practices.

According to recent reports, it may require replacing an operating system that has worked adequately for years. It may also mean changing the responsibilities of respected executives or asking local teams to adopt practices developed elsewhere in the enterprise.

Recent findings suggest that it may also require resisting the temptation to standardize activities that rely on local relationships and judgment. The objective should be neither to preserve acquired companies exactly as they were nor to eliminate their differences in pursuit of corporate uniformity.

It should be to develop organizations that can achieve what their constituent businesses could not accomplish independently.

The returns earned by companies that participated in homebuilding’s consolidation era will not reflect the ultimate opportunity. American homebuilding remains a uniquely complex process of converting land, capital, materials, labor, knowledge, and time into a finished product that households can purchase. Every unnecessary delay, redundant process, avoidable error, excessive handoff, and poorly coordinated decision adds cost somewhere along that process.

Some of those costs are so sticky they seem almost unavoidable. Others reflect operating practices that have persisted through the decades because the industry has struggled to coordinate the many participants involved in building a home.

Larger enterprises with better information, stronger leadership, deeper technical capabilities, and greater capacity to invest in improvement can change that.

The goal should be a homebuilding value stream that produces more value with less wasted time, effort, and expense, i.e., less “stream.”.

Better execution will not, by itself, overcome high land prices, expensive financing, restrictive regulation, infrastructure constraints, or the gap between household incomes and housing costs. Those barriers remain substantial. But homebuilders have meaningful control over how they organize their businesses and how efficiently they turn resources into finished homes.

It has been revealed that the industry’s era of consolidation has brought together an enormous collection of land assets, operating organizations, local relationships, and management talent under larger ownership platforms. What happens next will determine whether those combinations yield more than additional market share and purchasing leverage.

The most key measure of homebuilding’s great acquisition era may ultimately have little to do with how many companies changed hands or how much their buyers paid.

It may be how much better those enterprises become at converting land, capital, talent, and knowledge into homes that more American households can afford.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin mining giant MARA Holdings, formerly known as Marathon Digital, continues to offload its Bitcoin holdings, with another multimillion-dollar transfer spotted as the company's selling spree shows no signs of slowing down.
  • Recent findings suggest that according to blockchain analytics platform Lookonchain, MARA transferred another 366 BTC, worth approximately $23.33 million, from its wallets on Nov.
  • The latest transaction follows a series of substantial Bitcoin sales by the mining organization throughout 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin mining giant MARA Holdings, formerly known as Marathon Digital, continues to offload its Bitcoin holdings, with another multimillion-dollar transfer spotted as the company's selling spree shows no signs of slowing down.

Recent findings suggest that according to blockchain analytics platform Lookonchain, MARA transferred another 366 BTC, worth approximately $23.33 million, from its wallets on Nov. 18.

The latest transaction follows a series of substantial Bitcoin sales by the mining organization throughout 2026.

Lookonchain estimates that MARA has already sold a staggering 40,581 BTC this year, generating approximately $3.03 billion at an average selling price of $74,446 per coin.

However, it remains unclear whether the latest 366 BTC transfer represents another completed sale or an internal movement of funds.

MARA's aggressive selling strategy is confirmed by its latest quarterly financial disclosures.

According to its Nov. 9 SEC filing, the company sold approximately 26,984 BTC for $1.9 billion during the first nine months of 2026.

Following the end of September, MARA liquidated another 13,597 BTC at an average price of approximately $81,039, raising an additional $1.1 billion.

These transactions bring its total disclosed Bitcoin sales to 40,581 BTC.

Notably, the tech giant used $750 million from its latest sales to fully repay Bitcoin-backed loans, releasing 17,477 BTC previously pledged as collateral.

Interestingly, MARA has explicitly signaled that it intends to continue selling Bitcoin as part of a broader shift in its corporate strategy.

However, it began allowing sales of newly mined Bitcoin in 2025 before expanding the policy in 2026 to include coins already held on its balance sheet.

In its latest shareholder letter, MARA said it plans to continue monetizing Bitcoin to strengthen its financial flexibility.

The manufacturer specifically identified artificial intelligence infrastructure, upcoming convertible debt obligations and potential share repurchases as reasons for building up cash reserves.

The selling comes as MARA faces considerable pressure on its core mining business.

Third-quarter revenue declined 35% year over year to $164.2 million, compared to $252.4 million in the corresponding period of 2025.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:38 pm.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella opened his Ignite keynote Tuesday in San Francisco by addressing the elephant in the room: the global Outlook outage that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries last week.

Before getting to Copilot, agents or any of the event’s news, Nadella said the outage was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure has become as “the dial tone for the world.”.

Sources indicate that “We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously,” he noted. “And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve.”.

The line drew applause from the crowd, interrupting Nadella as he moved to thank the IT pros in the audience who kept their own organizations running through the outage.

In a recent development, it was a brief acknowledgment, and he didn’t go into what went wrong. Microsoft’s preliminary report blamed a bug in a fix it began rolling out in July, which its own automatic rerouting spread until most of the servers in a key Microsoft 365 gateway stopped responding. A final report is due Nov. 20.

Industry observers note that from there, Nadella moved on to the main show. Watch the keynote below, and see updates here.

#121965. Why aren’t mortgage rates lower after massive stock sell-off?

Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Why aren’t mortgage rates lower after massive stock sell-off?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (658 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, AI stocks have sold off and oil prices are lower, but the 10-year yield is at 4.94% and mortgage rates are still abouve 7.30%.
  • It has been revealed that the Federal Reserve has been worried about oil prices driving inflation since the Iran conflict began and has noted that the trade war inflation has mostly been passed through.
  • Sources indicate that I talked about this on the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor-in-Chief Sarah Wheeler, but with today’s market action, I need to revisit this question with some charts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, AI stocks have sold off and oil prices are lower, but the 10-year yield is at 4.94% and mortgage rates are still abouve 7.30%. So what gives?

It has been revealed that the Federal Reserve has been worried about oil prices driving inflation since the Iran conflict began and has noted that the trade war inflation has mostly been passed through. Now AI stocks are being slammed, with moratoriums on data centers coming in the near future as the anti-AI backlash grows. In this environment, you could expect the 10-year yield and rates to fall, but that’s not what’s happening.

Sources indicate that I talked about this on the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor-in-Chief Sarah Wheeler, but with today’s market action, I need to revisit this question with some charts. Let’s go over each part of this storyline.

Industry observers note that oil prices were very volatile earlier this year and bond yields started moving in synch with them — especially after the first MOU deal broke off. Now that oil prices have fallen, you might expect at least a few Federal Reserve members to say that this could be a positive, but they haven’t.

In fact, when oil was trading between $68-$82, no Fed members stated anything positive, and Cleveland Fed President (and Fed hawk) Beth Hammack talked about how lower oil prices were were actually bad for inflation because people could then spend more money.

It has been revealed that in any case, so far, lower oil prices haven’t helped the 10-year yield get below 4.70%. If oil can trade between $67-$82, that would help a lot, but the last time that happened was when we declared a deal with Iran in June.

In a recent development, I have used the CoreWeave stock price as an example of the problems with the AI companies. Since CoreWeave had some financing concerns, the markets have soured on AI, and as you can see in the chart below, the manufacturer’s stock price has been crushed. This has helped keep the 10-year yield below 5.35% for sure and has assisted in lower yields this week. But we are still elevated versus what we saw after the MOU deal was announced.

The Fed has made AI a huge inflation talking point, and they need to see much more pain in the AI sector before changing their tune.

Industry observers note that if we were getting all this news about AI and oil prices four weeks ago, I believe the 10-year yield and mortgage rates would be lower today. But all this stock drama and falling oil prices came in a 14-day period where the Fed hawks came out every day talking about more Fed rate hikes, even a 50-basis-point hike. I mean, look at how the U.S. dollar hasn’t been fazed by the market drama.

Sources indicate that for the past two months, I have focused on two key levels for the 10-year yield: 5.35% and 5.15%. Both those levels held and yields have fallen from these points. So what lower oil prices and falling stocks have done is made sure bond yields don’t go much higher and for now, let’s take that as a victory. However, I do understand why people might be scratching their heads on why rates aren’t lower with lower oil prices and falling AI stocks.

Sources indicate that the Fed hawks are the main reason bond yields aren’t lower; they want to make sure that the bond market doesn’t get relaxed, even with lower oil prices and falling stocks, and they have done their job well. They really want to take back all the insurance interest rate cuts from last year and because of this, the 10-year yield is still at 4.95%. If the Fed members weren’t so hawkish over the last two weeks, bond yields would be lower and we would have already had sub-7% mortgage rates.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • is reportedly in talks to buy Zscaler Inc., a publicly traded provider of cybersecurity software.
  • Sources told Bloomberg today that the acquisition could “come together soon.” However, they cautioned that it’s still possible the talks will fall through.
  • Investors seem to be confident that the deal will materialize.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:50 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. is reportedly in talks to buy Zscaler Inc., a publicly traded provider of cybersecurity software.

Sources told Bloomberg today that the acquisition could “come together soon.” However, they cautioned that it’s still possible the talks will fall through.

Investors seem to be confident that the deal will materialize. Zscaler’s share price jumped more than 16% in after-hours trading, while CrowdStrike dropped about 4.8%.

In a recent development, software buyouts tend to value the acquired company at a premium to its last unaffected market capitalization. As a result, CrowdStrike is likely to pay more than the $32 billion Zscaler was worth at the end of today’s trading session. That means the deal could take CrowdStrike’s market capitalization above $250 billion.

According to recent reports, crowdStrike sells one of the world’s most popular cybersecurity platforms. Falcon can detect and block malicious activity across cloud instances, on-premises servers, employee devices and other assets. It also automates certain related tasks, such as finding sensitive records that are stored in an insecure manner.

Zscaler competes in a different part of the cybersecurity market. It sells software that protects the network connections through which a firm’s employees access its business applications.

According to recent reports, enterprises historically used virtual private network, or VPN, tools for that task. Such programs tend to be quite slow. More significantly, they give employees access to the entire corporate network rather than to the specific applications they need for their work. That broad access can create cybersecurity risks.

Industry observers note that zscaler sells a zero-trust network access, or ZTNA, platform designed to replace legacy VPN software. It limits the number of applications that workers can access within the corporate network. If Zscaler detects risky activity, it asks the affected user to complete additional authentication steps.

The firm’s ZTNA software doubles as an observability tool. Administrators can monitor employees’ connections for technical complications that may hinder productivity. A built-in artificial intelligence assistant, the ZDX Agent, generates troubleshooting advice.

It has been revealed that zscaler also competes in other product categories where CrowdStrike has a limited presence. Notably, it offers a tool that deploys bogus applications, user passwords and files in customer networks. Those simulated assets act as sensors. When an attempt is made to access one of them, Zscaler Deception notifies the customer that a cyberattack is underway.

The potential deal would mark CrowdStrike’s largest acquisition by a wide margin. The company’s biggest buyout to date is its $970 million purchase of startup SGNL Inc., which closed earlier this year. The deal bought CrowdStrike a platform that can automatically end users’ application sessions when it detects cybersecurity issues.

Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has said that crypto needs some of the features that made housing a safe investment for earlier generations. "We need the equivalent of those good properties that housing investment has, for modern digital assets," Buterin wrote in a post on X on Nov. 18.

The post came a day after economist Peter Tulip published his own post on housing in Raleigh, North Carolina. According to Tulip, looser zoning rules in the city set off a construction boom and pushed real rents down 15% between 2022 and 2025.

In his post, Buterin first pointed to a benefit of young people putting their savings into stocks and crypto instead of real estate.

"One benefit of younger generations investing more in stonks and other digital things instead of housing is that it reduces perverse incentives that drive people to push to keep housing expensive, instead of rejoicing when prices drop as we do for all other life necessities," he wrote.

According to recent reports, still, the Ethereum co-founder noted that housing has had one advantage over stocks and crypto. He described it as "a culture and policy-encouraged default of investing in a safe non-crazy thing that you can't easily liquidate.".

"Modern platforms encourage the opposite of this, leading to more irresponsible behavior," Buterin added.

Ether was trading at $1,808 on Wednesday.

Sources indicate that buterin has written about housing and urban planning before. He has supported the YIMBY movement for denser development in cities for several years.

In 2022, Buterin argued for a land value tax. According to him, such a tax would lower the upfront cost of buying a home and discourage speculation on vacant lots.

In 2025, the Ethereum co-founder called the housing market a "confusing market of peculiar NFTs." According to Buterin, what is really being sold under the label of square footage is the right to live in a particular city. At the time, he also said that legalizing dense development speeds up the economy and benefits even people who prefer single-family homes.

According to recent reports, ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse believes the recent crypto market sell-off stems largely from investors rotating capital into high-profile initial public offerings. The Ripple boss and crypto billionaire anticipates a recovery once Anthropic’s massive listing is fully absorbed.

Speaking to CNBC on November 19th, Garlinghouse drew a direct parallel to SpaceX’s public debut earlier in the year. He explained that when major IPOs generate intense demand, investors often sell liquid assets such as Bitcoin and XRP to free up cash for share subscriptions.

The same pattern, he said, unfolded ahead of Anthropic’s offering. After SpaceX completed its listing, crypto markets staged a notable rebound. Garlinghouse expects a similar bounce this time.

Anthropic, the artificial-intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot family, has priced its IPO at $83 per share, above the previously marketed range of $70 to $78.

The deal ranks among the largest IPOs in history, raising tens of billions of dollars and valuing the manufacturer in the trillion-dollar range, and shares are set to begin trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.

Industry observers note that such blockbuster offerings typically attract enormous institutional and retail interest, temporarily diverting capital from other risk assets. Once the primary allocation is complete and secondary-market trading stabilizes, some of that capital often flows back into crypto and other liquid markets.

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin had slipped near $62,000 on Wednesday before recovering above $63,000 early Thursday. Garlinghouse framed the dip as a temporary capital-rotation effect rather than a fundamental loss of confidence in digital assets. He also expressed confidence that Anthropic’s shares would trade strongly given the strong demand and pricing above the range.

In a recent development, looking further ahead, Garlinghouse remained optimistic about blockchain’s long-term role. He predicted that within roughly a decade, blockchain technology will be deeply embedded across global financial infrastructure, much as artificial intelligence has already transformed multiple industries.

His comments highlight how large technology IPOs can create short-term pressure on crypto while potentially reinforcing longer-term narratives around innovation and capital markets.

Will the AI stock sell-off give us sub-7% mortgage rates before the holidays?

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sub-7% mortgage rates are back on the holiday menu!
  • In the 2026 HousingWire forecast, I anticipated the following ranges:.
  • If all this market drama happened four weeks ago, I believe the 10-year yield would be under 4.85% today, but this is happening amid a rapid-fire, two-week effort by the Federal Reserve to give forward-guidance about more rate hikes coming in the system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sub-7% mortgage rates are back on the holiday menu! Just when it looked like we had no chance for a happy holiday, AI stocks are still taking a beating and pushing money into bonds. Oil prices almost went below $80 last week too. We have three holidays left before 2027 kicks into gear, so the question now is: Can we get the 10-year yield and mortgage spreads low enough to get lower mortgage rates?

In the 2026 HousingWire forecast, I anticipated the following ranges:.

If all this market drama happened four weeks ago, I believe the 10-year yield would be under 4.85% today, but this is happening amid a rapid-fire, two-week effort by the Federal Reserve to give forward-guidance about more rate hikes coming in the system. The key level of 5.15% for the 10-year yield held last week, and with the AI sell-off and oil prices down to $83 again, we have a shot to get sub-7% mortgage rates again, but that will require the 10-year yield to get to 4.85% and head lower — and for mortgage spreads to improve back down toward 2%.Mortgage rates have had a difficult time lately with the inflation data and the Fed’s hawkish tone. In addition, we still don’t have a resolution to the Iran conflict, and when President Trump talks about bigger tariffs with our partners, it makes it harder for yields to go down. We also have to be mindful that inflation is rising while the unemployment rate is falling; if those two things change, it will be better for rates. For now, let’s focus on getting rates lower before the holidays. What can get us there?1. Stocks selling off almost got us to 4.85% again; we got as low as 4.92% Friday. The problem is the speed of the decline doesn’t help mortgage spreads. However, if we see more market selling, that can be one positive variable.2. Any positive news on the Iran conflict or limiting the trade war.3. The hope that the Democrats will resolve the conflict and trade war after Jan. 3 might get bond traders and oil traders thinking differently.We don’t have much time before the end-of-year holidays, but the above will help. However, the reverse is also true: stocks rallying, the conflict getting worse or more negative trade war headlines can lead yields and rates higher.

Mortgage spreads have recently gotten worse, which is a big variable in why rates got as high as 7.60% recently, but they’re still close to multiyear lows. We need less volatility in the bond markets, and with time, the spreads can improve again. Since September, the markets have been a bit too wild, rising and falling, and the spreads’ job is to reduce mortgage rate volatility. A big key for mortgage rates to get below 7% is getting the spreads back to 2% and under.

It has been revealed that historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads rose to 2.18% from 2.15% a week earlier.

Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been at the best spread levels this year and the worst levels of this cycle.

Recent findings suggest that our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data.

Recent findings suggest that we saw slight week-to-week growth last week and housing data has really stabilized in the recent weeks; however, I would just view this as an adjustment to the rate shock we saw when rates moved from 6.75% to 7.60%, and demand got noticeably hit. The year-over-year comps are going to be difficult for some time, as mortgage rates were much lower last year than today.Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years:.

Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. Rates rose aggressively during inflation week, so this data line did get hit, down 3% week-to-week and down 18% year-over-year. Again, the year-over-year comps here are rough, as mortgage rates were a lot lower last year. Earlier in the year, all we had was positive year-over-year, but rates reached the range where housing data slows down, and the comps have been very difficult.

Here are the stats on purchase apps so far in 2026:.

In a recent development, housing inventory had a slight decline last week and is in its seasonal decline for 2026, as the peak in inventory already happened. Inventory growth did pick up when mortgage rates headed toward 7.60%; before that, inventory growth was slow this year, and we even had some weeks when inventory was negative year-over-year. Until mid-June it was hard for the comps to show growth this year and now they’re much easier to show growth as housing demand was heading toward a nine-month high last year this time.

Inventory growth is running at 8.12%.

It has been revealed that upcoming listings have been in their seasonal decline since June, and nothing abnormal with this data line has happened in 2026; in fact, it’s been the best year of new listings since early 2022. One concern always with higher rates is that sellers will decide not to put their homes on the market; that has not happened this year, which is a positive sign for housing.In a normal environment, new listings range from 80,000 to 100,000 per week during peak periods. For context, during the housing bubble years, new listings ranged from 250,000 to 400,000 per week for several years.Here is last week’s new listings data for the past two years:.

Typically, about one-third of homes see price reductions before they sell, reflecting the housing market’s dynamic nature. Overall, price-cut percentages this year have been lower than last year. This held true until rates moved above 6.64% and then above 7%. At that point, demand fell, and the year-over-year price-cut percentage rose 1%, and last week the year-over-year price-cut gap was 2% higher than last year when demand was picking up with lower rates.In my 2026 home-price forecast, I called for a national decline of -0.62% for the year. Home-price growth really isn’t going anywhere this year, and my -0.62% forecast is going to have a hard time being right this year. I simply don’t have enough time to be correct, as most of the year prices have been rising roughly 1%-2 % with the Case-Shiller Index. It’s only recently that we can see some negative year-over-year data, and we only have a few weeks left in the year.The price-cut percentage for last week:.

It’s Thanksgiving week, so this means we can see some crazy volatility with stocks and bonds — and some hours with not a lot of volume. Next week’s tracker will obviously be hit by the holidays. However, this week we do have some economic data that can move the markets. PCE inflation, newly introduced home sales, PMI and other reports will add to the mix of volatility. And who knows what “upgrades” might shut down another institution or part of our infrastructure from operating normally this week!

Seattle tech vet and Sounders FC minority owner Chee Chew joins front office to lead AI push

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (946 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:02 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:02 am.
  • Industry observers note that chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon.
  • Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club announced Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:02 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:02 am.

Industry observers note that chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon. Now the Seattle tech veteran is taking on a newly introduced job with the Sounders and Reign FC, where he’ll lead how the soccer clubs use technology, data and AI.

Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club announced Tuesday.

“His knowledge of and passion for the Sounders and Reign allow him to hit the ground running,” Hanauer said in a statement. “His experience leading teams through major shifts in technology gives us a unique opportunity to strengthen both the soccer and business sides of our organization.”.

According to recent reports, chew most recently was chief product and technology officer at Zapier, where he helped steer the workflow automation company toward AI. Before that he was chief product officer at mParticle and at Twilio, where he oversaw the communications company’s $3.2 billion acquisition of Segment.

He spent four years at Amazon, nearly eight years as a vice president of engineering at Google, where he also led the manufacturer’s Seattle and Kirkland offices, and 14 years at Microsoft working on Internet Explorer, Windows Mobile and Xbox Live.

In a recent development, chew said his direct team will stay small, but its work will reach every corner of the business, including HR, ticket sales, customer service, match-day planning, corporate partnerships, legal, and player recruiting and scouting. He also wants every department to have its own “builders,” staffers who can create AI tools and automations for their own teams.

“In order to do a change like this, it’s more than technology,” Chew told GeekWire. “Technology is in many ways the easiest part. Driving change, getting deep, building side by side with folks, I think is what it takes.”.

Chew didn’t grow up playing soccer. “My family was a very traditional Chinese family of study and play piano,” he said. “It was a stereotype, but it was true for my family.” He caught the bug in college, where he played a ton of intramurals, and later from his wife, Christine, who played through college, and their two kids.

According to recent reports, the couple joined the Sounders ownership group in 2019 as one of 11 Seattle-rooted families, many with deep ties to the region’s tech industry. Former Microsoft executive Terry Myerson pulled the group together, and it included Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, CFO Amy Hood, and others.

A group of owners has met every other Friday since 2019, and “leveraging technology has always been part of the strategy” for the club, Chew remarked.

The job grew out of a demo Chew built for Hanauer about two and a half years ago: an AI agent that could handle complicated fan requests, such as a season ticket holder with four seats who wants to buy a block of eight. The club later brought in consultants to train staff on AI, but the effort never quite gained momentum, he mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that talks about a bigger role started early this year and came together by midyear. “Adrian and I talked about it, and we agreed for me to come on board and take an operational role and hack on some code,” Chew said.

Chew describes Hanauer as a visionary on “the art of the possible” who comes in daily asking, “Could you do this?” Recently, as Chew was boarding a flight home to Seattle, Hanauer called from a meeting where staff doubted they could scale up one effort tenfold without hiring more people. Could AI help?

Recent findings suggest that on the flight, while using the plane’s Wi-Fi, he built a prototype with Anthropic’s Claude. “By the time I landed, I sent it to them and remarked, ‘OK, give this a try,’” he said. The club used it in an experiment to scale up performance marketing before a match.

It’s the kind of hands-on building Chew notes he’s been doing a lot of lately.

“I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years,” he noted. “It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”.

Chew is also working with players.

According to recent reports, he recently ran an AI analysis of one player’s game, based on stats such as touches, expected goals and distance run. It pointed out strengths and areas to improve. The player was “very hungry for it,” Chew noted, and asked if they could do it every game.

The club’s performance analytics group, led by data analyst Tyler Cox, was already ahead of much of the organization, and Chew said he’s helping speed up that work with AI.

Recent findings suggest that the bigger challenge is getting people to change how they work, Chew remarked. At Zapier, he saw many companies struggle to get results from AI, with some spending “massive token budgets” without a significant win. He said the answer is blending AI with traditional automation and fitting it into how people already work.

Industry observers note that “It has to be approachable for folks,” he mentioned. “You can’t go in and just throw everything up and start from scratch.”.

The Sounders host Real Salt Lake in the wild-card round of the MLS Cup Playoffs on Thursday at Lumen Field. Asked whether AI could help figure out a win, Chew passed.

“I don’t want to get involved and interfere with our coaching staff,” he said.

  • MEXC confirmed that its Global Card service will be discontinued on November 18, according to the exchange's announcement.
  • Customers have two things to take care of before the service ends.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

MEXC confirmed that its Global Card service will be discontinued on November 18, according to the exchange's announcement. The tech giant cites service adjustments by its third-party card issuer. From the deadline, existing cards can no longer be used for transactions, and newly introduced card applications are suspended.

Customers have two things to take care of before the service ends.

First, the remaining card balance has to be withdrawn: the Withdraw button on the Global Card page sends the funds to the Fiat account.

According to recent reports, second, subscriptions linked to the card should be cancelled or switched to another payment method. Unfortunately for cardholders, recurring payments will most likely fail if they stay on the old card.

If there's still a balance when the service ends, MEXC will credit it to the Spot account, so people will simply receive their funds back. It's notable to keep in mind that pending card transactions need time to settle, which is why the balance snapshot comes on November 21, three days after the shutdown. The amount will be credited within three business days of the snapshot. Users do not need to take any action.

Refunds for previous card transactions will be credited to the Fiat account once MEXC receives them. Pending cashback will be credited automatically as scheduled. Elite VVIP customers with zero-fee benefits will be refunded too, though the eligible fees return to their Spot accounts only before December 15.

Transaction history, card orders and cashback records stay available on the Global Card page for three months after the service ends, so it's worth saving anything needed before access ends.

Cryptocurrency services delegate certain types of services to third parties all the time, so witnessing a similar situation is more than a possibility here. Realistically, the shutdown is somewhat inconvenient rather than dangerous, as the balances are returned automatically. For consumers: stay vigilant and try not to put all your eggs in one basket.

#121956. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

📅 30 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1278 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Nulltx ↗ Open Full Page

Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1278 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty.
  • Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.
  • Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Recent findings suggest that the OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

It has been revealed that the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to concern under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management.".

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:.

In a recent development, the OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

In a recent development, for existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

According to recent reports, the main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:.

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

According to recent reports, under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

In a recent development, the Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:.

In a recent development, the difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:.

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:.

Sources indicate that both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

Latest Update: Seattle police unleash dog-like robot whose best trick is bomb dispoal

💡 Key Takeaways
