📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bossing around an AI underling may yield better results than being polite, but that doesn’t mean a ruder tone won’t have consequences in the long run, researchers say.
  • A study from Penn State found ChatGPT’s 4o model produced better results on 50 multiple-choice questions as researchers’ prompts grew ruder.
  • Since then, Anthropic has moved to prohibit sustained cruelty toward its AI models, and the same researchers have found that prompt tone can also affect the computing resources AI consumes by as much as 44.3%.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bossing around an AI underling may yield better results than being polite, but that doesn’t mean a ruder tone won’t have consequences in the long run, researchers say.

A study from Penn State found ChatGPT’s 4o model produced better results on 50 multiple-choice questions as researchers’ prompts grew ruder.

Since then, Anthropic has moved to prohibit sustained cruelty toward its AI models, and the same researchers have found that prompt tone can also affect the computing resources AI consumes by as much as 44.3%.

In a recent development, in the original study from 2025, more than 250 unique prompts were sorted by politeness to rudeness, with the “very rude” response yielded an accuracy of 84.8%, four percentage points higher than the “very polite” response. Essentially, the LLM responded better when researchers gave it prompts like “Hey, gofer, figure this out,” than when they said “Would you be so kind as to solve the following question?”.

While ruder responses generally yielded more accurate responses, the researchers noted “uncivil discourse” could have unintended consequences.

“Using insulting or demeaning language in human-AI interaction could have negative effects on user experience, accessibility, and inclusivity, and may contribute to harmful communication norms,” the researchers wrote at the time.

At the time it was published, the preprint study, which has not been peer-reviewed, offered upcoming evidence that not only sentence structure, but tone, affects an AI chatbot’s responses—and that human’s interactions with AI may be more nuanced than they appeared on the surface.

Sources indicate that the Penn State researchers noted some limitations to their study, such as the relatively small sample size of responses and the study’s reliance mostly on one AI model, ChatGPT 4o, which is no longer available for most consumers. The researchers also noted it’s possible more advanced AI models would make tone considerations null. Still, the investigation added to the growing intrigue behind AI models and their intricacy..

In a recent development, “For the longest of times, we humans have wanted conversational interfaces for interacting with machines,” one author of the study, Penn State Information Systems professor Akhil Kumar Kumar told Fortune in an email in 2025. “But now we realize that there are drawbacks for such interfaces too and there is some value in APIs that are structured.”.

Industry observers note that since the original study, Kumar and fellow researcher Om Dobariya, a Ph.D. student in information systems at Penn State, have expanded their investigation, finding that the way people speak to AI chatbots can have an even greater impact on computing costs than on the accuracy of their responses.

In a July 2026 pre-print paper, which has also not been peer-reviewed, the same researchers tested four AI models, including OpenAI’s GPT-4o and GPT-5-nano and Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash and Flash-Lite, using 570 multiple-choice questions and seven different prompt tones ranging from sycophantic to threatening.

They found that output-token consumption, which reflects the amount of text a chatbot generates and can affect the cost of running AI models, varied by as much as 44.3% depending on the prompt’s tone. The differences in accuracy were smaller, but the study added credence to the idea that the tone humans take with AI could have implications for companies looking to reduce their computing costs.

“While earlier we had found that tone affects accuracy by a few percentage points,” Kumar told Fortune in an email this week, the more recent research found that tone shifted output-token consumption by up to 44.3%, “far more than the effect on accuracy.”.

“Rude, threatening language expressing urgency elicits shorter responses while polite, sycophantic inquiries produce longer answers incurring greater computational cost,” he added.

Kumar and Dobariya’s newest research comes as AI companies are increasingly considering how owners interact with their chatbots.

Recent findings suggest that in October, Anthropic declared an updated usage policy that took effect earlier in November banning “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models.” The organization clarified the restriction applies only to extreme cases involving repeated cruelty toward its AI models, and didn’t include ordinary frustration. The AI company went public this week with an IPO that raised a record-setting $93.5 billion.

Still, the newly introduced policy fits in with Anthropic’s existing policy of allowing Claude to end conversations with persistently abusive consumers, as well as Anthropic cofounder Chris Olah’s previous comments that AI models “functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease.”.

According to recent reports, “I can fully understand why Anthropic wishes to prohibit cruel speech,” Kumar told Fortune. “And, yes, indeed, LLMs do exhibit human-like, anthropomorphic tendencies, not to be confused with consciousness. They do react to social register, tone, and other aspects of speech.”.

Kumar remarked his latest findings suggest users may need to rethink how they talk to AI to save on computational costs.

“The default style should be neutral leaning towards firm to optimize the computation cost and result quality,” he added. “This would reduce wasteful compute and inference cost too.”.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on October 30, 2025.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Recent findings suggest that most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

According to recent reports, the schedule is fixed. Circle declared in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026.".

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

According to recent reports, circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the tech giant wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible.".

In a recent development, funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations.".

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1.".

Recent findings suggest that the main text above it notes something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:.

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:.

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

In a recent development, many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

Industry observers note that the fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:.

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

Industry observers note that for teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

According to recent reports, for everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • According to recent reports, A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten.
  • Industry observers note that I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

According to recent reports, A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he said, “but you can’t do both at once.”.

Industry observers note that I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a company.

We tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

I think about Jack’s line a lot this time of year, because the fourth quarter makes business owners a little crazy. The year is almost over, you’ve got revenue goals to hit, budgets to review, and everyone’s already asking about your prepares for next year. For a lot of founders, the natural response is to put their heads down and work harder. I’ve done it plenty of times myself, and I’ve learned that a lot of that extra effort goes into motion that never turns into progress.

According to recent reports, I’ve spent most of my career working with entrepreneurs building businesses in smaller markets. They know exactly when payroll hits, and they’re building their companies without millions of dollars in outside investment. For them, time is as tight as cash. A business like that can stay incredibly busy for years while nothing really changes.

So before the year wraps up, it’s worth asking a few uncomfortable questions to make sure your time and effort are actually moving you forward.

Industry observers note that revenue is important. I’m certainly not going to argue otherwise. But revenue alone can hide a lot. You can grow sales while your margins shrink. You can bring in new customers who are a nightmare to serve, or hire a bunch of people and add services only to discover you’ve built a more complicated version of the business you already had. I’ve watched founders post record sales and still end the year with less cash and less freedom than they started with.

Before you set another ambitious revenue target, look at what your growth is actually producing. Are you more profitable? Is your team getting stronger? Are your customers happier? Is the business becoming less dependent on you? Those questions will tell you a lot more about whether you’re building something that lasts.

Sources indicate that entrepreneurs are idea people. We love trying newly introduced things, whether it’s a new campaign or some shiny piece of software that promises to change everything (cough, cough, AI). I’m guilty of it, too. At some point, though, we have to be honest about the difference between what we enjoy doing and what moves the business forward.

It has been revealed that take marketing. You might spend hours making social media content because you enjoy it, while most of your best customers come from referrals. Or you might be convinced a particular service is your bread and butter, only to find out a less exciting offering is generating most of your profit. The numbers don’t always tell the story we want to hear.

Industry observers note that so figure out where your best customers are coming from and what they’re buying. A spreadsheet and an honest hour will get you most of the way there. And if you identify something that’s working, do more of it.

This might be my favorite question, because it’s where founders find the quickest wins.

Every business picks up habits over the years: Meetings that made sense two years ago, reports nobody reads, software nobody logs into, services that stay on the menu because they’ve always been there. Individually, none of these seem like a major deal. Added up, they eat a surprising amount of time and money, and they eat your attention, which might be the most valuable thing a founder has.

Sources indicate that look at what your team spends time on every week and ask a simple question: If we were starting this business today, would we still do it this way? If the answer is no, why are you doing it now?

According to recent reports, I love setting goals. I’m a substantial believer in having a vision and building a plan to get there. I’ve also learned that a fresh calendar year has never solved an old problem for me. If your sales process is broken in October, a fresh set of goals in January won’t fix it. If you’re spending money on marketing that doesn’t work, a bigger budget just means you’ll waste more of it. And if you’re the bottleneck in every decision, adding more customers is going to make your life harder.

For the first several years of Bolt, I was in every meeting. That made sense when we were scrappy and fighting for every account. As we grew, I started getting in the way of the systems we’d built to run without me. Now the question I ask my team constantly is, “Do I have to be in this meeting?” Usually the answer is no, and the business runs better because of it.

You don’t have to overhaul the whole manufacturer all at once. Pick one or two things that would make a real difference, like improving your margins, simplifying an offer, documenting a process or finally handing off something you’ve held onto for too long. Then make those changes now, while you still have some time left in the year.

There’s nothing wrong with pushing hard to finish the year strong. I hope you hit every goal you’ve set. Just don’t get so locked in on a number that you lose sight of what you’re building. Most of us started our businesses to create opportunity and have some control over our time and our future, and a bigger revenue line doesn’t guarantee either one.

Jack was right that you can’t do both at once. So before you lock in next year’s number, ask yourself which season you’re in. If it’s a season to get bigger, run. If it’s a season to get better, give yourself permission to slow down and fix what’s underneath. Either way, choose it on purpose.

A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he said, “but you can’t do both at once.”.

I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a manufacturer.

Sources indicate that we tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

Although Bitwise did not record any inflow or outflow on this day, the firm still stands as XRP’s biggest ETF manager as it controls over $392.64 million in net assets as of this date.

Despite its dominance in the XRP ETF market, Bitwise has remained muted all week, showing zero daily participation since November 9, when it posted its highest-ever daily outflow of $9.40 million.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:36 pmNovember 17, 2026 at 6:36 pm.

Jeff Bezos has a space tech giant, a newspaper, an AI startup that’s raised $14.5 billion and, apparently, a seat in the room when Amazon decides who gets a license to kill.

Speaking Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, the Amazon founder said he was “heavily involved” in the casting of Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond, a pick Amazon MGM Studios unveiled Monday.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond franchise when it acquired MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, then took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

Bezos said a large initial pool of would-be Bonds was narrowed to five finalists, who then did “real old-fashioned screen tests”: three scenes apiece, in full costume on real sets with other actors.

The other finalists were Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner, according to The Upcoming York Times, which reported that the tests took place in London in late October.

Bezos stated the decision-makers got together Friday and spent a couple of hours reviewing the screen tests before settling on Pattinson.

“By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing,” Bezos remarked. “But there was something special about Rob Pattinson and his performances.” He said the group, including director Denis Villeneuve, reached a quick consensus. It was “kind of immediately undebated.”.

Bezos admitted that the group was initially “slightly biased” against Pattinson because he’s already so famous.

According to recent reports, “We sort of thought, you know, maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown,” he mentioned. “But in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”.

Sources indicate that A sovereign AI factory is only as valuable as the companies that can actually get onto it. Across Europe, publicly funded AI factories are racing to give startups and small manufacturers supercomputer-class GPUs without pushing them into lock-in or loose data handling.

It has been revealed that in Stuttgart, the HammerHAI AI factory is taking shape around a system from Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. using Nvidia Corp. Grace Blackwell chips. The center’s pitch leans as much on people as on processors, according to Bastian Koller (pictured), managing director of the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart.

“It’s very notable to bring them there because everybody’s talking about AI, but we focus especially on SMEs and startups,” Koller remarked. “So some startups know what they want, some startups want to try and they need help and support.”.

According to recent reports, koller spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Amit Eyal Govrin at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how HammerHAI avoids lock-in, its pragmatic approach to sovereignty and a concierge model that pairs each customer with a consistent contact. (* Disclosure below.).

Industrial owners no longer want shell programming; they expect the look and feel of a hyperscaler, which raises fresh demands on security and access. The center has already worked with customers on existing systems while it waits on the fresh hardware, and several have produced success stories. Rather than holding onto them, it designs its services so workloads can leave, according to Koller.

“The idea is to evolve the system and the services in a way that they can simply move from us to a hyperscaler or from hyperscaler back,” Koller remarked. “Because what we are doing is, we give them a boost, we push them forward.”.

That pragmatism extends to sovereignty itself. The Stuttgart center runs an ISO-certified environment with TISAX Level 3 certification for automotive work. Full independence, down to European chips, is not realistic in the near term, Koller explained.

It has been revealed that “We cannot now say, okay, come back in 10 years when we have a sovereign processor or a sovereign GPU or something like this,” Koller remarked. “We have to look for the data.”.

Efficiency is part of the equation, too. The newly introduced system doubles the performance of its 3.2-megawatt predecessor at about 700 kilowatts, and the center reuses its waste heat. The bigger lesson is human: A concierge model pairs each customer with a consistent contact, according to Koller.

Sources indicate that “We learn more how the users are working and thinking, to be honest,” Koller noted. “… We can build up a system which is highly fancy, whatever there, nobody will use it because we never thought about what the user needs.”.

#121924. Vertex’s executive chairman: Here’s how we got our drug-trial success rate over 70% when the industry’s is 10% to 20%

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1156 w)

Vertex’s executive chairman: Here’s how we got our drug-trial success rate over 70% when the industry’s is 10% to 20%

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1156 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Corporate America is locked in an innovation arms race – a race that is turning out very few winners.
  • But more bets don’t necessarily produce more successes.
  • It has been revealed that there’s no more extreme example of this problem than pharmaceuticals and biotech.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Corporate America is locked in an innovation arms race – a race that is turning out very few winners. Companies are spending billions on R&D, acquisitions and new technologies, operating on the seemingly intuitive premise that making more bets is the best way to approach the uncertainty of the future.

But more bets don’t necessarily produce more successes.

It has been revealed that there’s no more extreme example of this problem than pharmaceuticals and biotech. It takes an average of 10 to 15 years for a drug to go from the lab to regulatory approval. And more than 90% of drugs that enter clinical development fail. Just look at the headlines: one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical companies recently suffered three drug trial failures in a single week despite an enormous R&D budget, many talented scientists and a deep pipeline.

But this problem is far from unique to healthcare. In consumer tech, many startups flame out after a single hit; in automotive, EV pioneers are routinely outpaced by fast followers; digital investments in retail often fail to translate into customer growth.

The instinctive response when innovation fails is to do more of it: fund more projects, pursue more ideas, make more acquisitions and place more bets. If innovation is inherently unpredictable, the thinking goes, the best way to improve your chances of success is to increase the number of shots you take.

Industry observers note that this kind of thinking is completely backward. It’s not about the shots. It’s about the target.

Imagine entering a darts tournament and throwing five consecutive bull’s-eyes, only to discover that you have been throwing at the wrong board. Your accuracy doesn’t matter. You’ve lost.

According to recent reports, more activity creates the appearance of innovation without improving its effectiveness. I learned this the hard way.

When I joined Vertex Pharmaceuticals in 2009, the company had spent two decades investing heavily in R&D across 20 different programs. Yet, it produced only a single breakthrough product, which was rendered obsolete just two and a half years later with the approval of a better and more tolerable treatment discovered by another company.

When we examined why drug development failed so frequently, the problem wasn’t that scientists had failed to create a drug that hit its intended biological target. The problem was that they had chosen the wrong target in the first place.

The solution was to take away choices, constraining ourselves to a “sandbox” of diseases with genetically- or pharmacologically-validated targets where we believed we had a much higher probability of success.

According to recent reports, most importantly, both R&D and business development had to stay inside the same sandbox. A fascinating scientific discovery or enticing acquisition wasn’t enough. If it didn’t fit our strategy or if we didn’t have a validated target to address, we walked away.

That last part may be the most difficult lesson for any leader. Companies often celebrate the ability to say yes to innovation. Sustainable innovators also become very good at saying no. Focus and strategy don’t limit innovation, they accelerate it.

A thriving innovation program requires many parts of an organization working in harmony. Yet companies unintentionally divide innovation into functional silos, with each group incentivized differently and no one focused on the big picture.

It has been revealed that researchers discover something and hand it to developers. Developers hand it to manufacturing. Eventually, commercial teams are asked to sell it. Business development may operate on a separate track entirely, hunting for external opportunities.

But a brilliant invention that cannot be efficiently developed, manufactured or commercialized isn’t a successful innovation.

To break down internal silos, leaders from research, development, regulatory, manufacturing, commercial and other key business units should be included in decisions about latest product development from the earliest stages of the innovation process. And internal and external innovation must be tightly integrated into the same strategy. Business development can’t be given permission to roam the universe looking for any interesting assets; partnerships and acquisitions must reinforce the same strategy, diseases, and targets where a manufacturer believes it has a high probability of success.

Industry observers note that innovation shouldn’t be measured by how many ideas an organization generates. It should be judged by how effectively the entire organization converts its best ideas into products that meet people’s needs and create meaningful value.

Recent findings suggest that once innovation succeeds, companies tend to become complacent and stop innovating to create better and better medicines for the same disease. Our experience seeing one of our breakthrough drugs promptly made obsolete by an innovative competitor created a sense of urgency, and even some paranoia, which drove our organization to continuously try to “out-innovate ourselves.”.

Being first doesn’t guarantee long term success. Competitors will learn from your breakthroughs and improve on the foundations you laid. We decided that if someone was going to build a better second-generation product, it should be us.

Sources indicate that the results were dramatic. Vertex went on to develop multiple transformative medicines, including 5 medicines that alter the course of cystic fibrosis for 95% of patients and, with CRISPR Therapeutics, the first FDA-approved human gene-editing therapy for patients with severe Sickle Cell Disease and transfusion-dependent B-thalassemia. More recently we created a completely newly introduced class of non-opioid medicines for moderate to severe acute pain.

Industry observers note that even more important to me is what happened to the odds. Our R&D success rate, measured by positive Phase II proof of concept, exceeded 70% across six diseases — far above the 10% to 20% industry average. We didn’t eliminate risk. Innovation can’t exist without risk. But we became much more deliberate about which risks were worth taking and therefore more successful.

Recent findings suggest that before approving the next project, acquisition or moonshot, leadership teams should ask themselves an vital set of questions: Do we understand why innovation has failed here before? Are we pursuing opportunities where we possess a genuine advantage? What evidence tells us that the underlying problem is solvable? Does this opportunity reinforce our existing capabilities – or merely distract from them? And, perhaps hardest of all, what are we willing to stop doing so that our best ideas have the resources to succeed?

Sources indicate that the innovation economy has conditioned leaders to admire the size of the pipeline, the number of experiments and the volume of bets. Those are measures of activity, not success.

Recent findings suggest that the companies that sustainably innovate will not be the ones willing to make the most bets. They’ll be the ones that understand their odds better than anyone else and have the discipline to walk away when those odds aren’t good enough.

Industry observers note that speaking during a keynote session titled 'The UAE's voice to the world' on the second day of the Ajman Media Forum 2026, 'THE SIGNAL', His Excellency described the forum's central question, 'Who owns the signal?', as one of the most profound questions of our time. His Excellency explained that the global media landscape is changing at an unprecedented pace, with digital platforms shaping public awareness and attitudes. He added that owning media platforms is no longer sufficient, and reach alone is no measure of influence. Those who own the signal today, he noted, are those who understand change, know their audiences, and present a comprehensive national narrative with a clear vision and message.

Recent findings suggest that H.E. Alshamsi emphasized the importance of communication tools in modern diplomacy, explaining that building trust now extends beyond dialogue forums and bilateral meetings to encompass media engagement. Audiences, he noted, look beyond official statements to images, stories, and positions.

According to recent reports, his Excellency affirmed that, under the leadership of His Highness Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, President of the UAE, the country recognized this shift early and adopted a forward-looking vision. It has made media an essential partner in Emirati diplomacy, conveying its message of dialogue, tolerance, coexistence, and openness to the world. His Excellency added that these national efforts call for the continuous development of public diplomacy tools and stronger partnerships with the media sector. Today's diplomats need the tools of media professionals, while media professionals need a diplomat's understanding of contexts and positions.

Recent findings suggest that in closing, His Excellency expressed his hope that the Ajman Media Forum would generate insights and practical initiatives that establish a upcoming phase of closer cooperation between diplomacy and media. These efforts, he remarked, would strengthen the UAE's international presence and influence, further consolidate its reputation and standing across global forums, and reinforce its position as a model for development and innovation and an active regional and international partner.

The 5 Little Habits That Made a Bigger Difference in My Business Than I Expected

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that when people talk about growing a business, they usually focus on the major moves: landing a major client, launching a fresh service or hiring the right team.
  • Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote, “The first wealth is health.” I didn’t fully appreciate that until I saw how much my energy, focus and decisions depended on how well I took care of myself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Industry observers note that when people talk about growing a business, they usually focus on the major moves: landing a major client, launching a fresh service or hiring the right team. But when I look back at my own journey, some of the things that helped me most were much smaller and easier to overlook.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote, “The first wealth is health.” I didn’t fully appreciate that until I saw how much my energy, focus and decisions depended on how well I took care of myself. That’s why I’m starting with the health habits that changed how I work, before moving on to the habits tied directly to running my business.

None of these were clever strategies or major investments. They were simple habits I built into my everyday routine. On their own, each one seemed minor. Over time, together, they made a real difference. Here are the little habits that I personally believe helped my business the most.

Recent findings suggest that one of the simplest habits that made a surprisingly major difference in my business was walking every day. When I first started spending long hours behind my laptop, I could easily go through an entire day barely moving. Eventually, I realized that waiting for free time to exercise wasn’t working, so I decided to make walking part of my daily routine.

The more I thought about it, the more I noticed how many people around me had the same problem. Founders, freelancers, marketers: Most of us spend our days at a desk and tell ourselves we’ll be more active once work slows down. But that moment rarely comes, and the effects build up quietly. According to Okdermo, about 41.9% of American adults are affected by obesity. There are many reasons behind that number, but a lack of daily movement is one of them, and it’s something I could actually control. I didn’t want my work to slowly become the reason my health got worse. Walking was the easiest way I found to change that, and I didn’t have to rebuild my whole schedule to do it.

And it turns out that you don’t need an extreme daily step count to see meaningful health benefits. According to Solace, walking 7,000 steps a day was associated with a 47% lower risk of death from any cause compared with walking 2,000 steps. Personally, I aim for around 15,000 steps a day, not because I believe it’s some magic number, but because I’ve noticed that I feel better, sleep more soundly and think more clearly when I reach it. Everyone should find a daily step count that works for their own body and lifestyle rather than blindly following someone else’s target.

Over time, my walks have also become some of the most productive parts of my day. I listen to podcasts, think through ideas and sometimes even take calls and meetings while I walk. I record voice memos and jot down notes whenever something useful comes to mind. Walking and talking at the same time helps me let go of stress, but more importantly, it clears my head. Some of my best business decisions were made not at my desk, but halfway through a walk.

Business impact: Walking helps me clear my mind, solve problems faster and make better business decisions.

Industry observers note that walking was a great start, but I knew I needed more than daily steps to stay in good shape. The problem was that I used to skip workouts whenever work got busy. There was always another deadline or client who needed my attention. That’s why I decided to hire a personal trainer. I knew that having someone waiting for me would make it harder to find excuses.

And it worked. According to PersonalTrainers, 88.2% of people training with in-person supervision met their workout attendance target, compared with 52.2% of those training on their own. Having someone hold me accountable made all the difference.

Sources indicate that now I treat workouts like client meetings. I put them on my calendar and rarely cancel. I’ve learned that sometimes the best way to stay consistent is to make a commitment to someone other than yourself.

Business impact: Working with a trainer helps me stay disciplined, manage my schedule better and maintain the energy I need to run my business.

According to recent reports, taking care of my health gave me more energy and focus, but some of the habits that made the biggest difference were directly tied to how I run my business. One of them was giving more attention to existing clients instead of constantly chasing latest ones. Early on, I was so focused on winning new projects that I sometimes overlooked the people who were already paying for my services. Eventually, I realized that building long-term relationships was far more valuable than constantly starting from scratch.

Sources indicate that I began listening more carefully, communicating more openly and looking for ways to deliver more than clients expected. The results have been worth it: Today, clients stay with my business for an average of 3.5 years. And the financial value of retention shouldn’t be underestimated. According to Coruzant, even a 5% improvement in customer retention can increase profits by 25% or more. For me, that reinforces why taking better care of existing clients deserves just as much attention as bringing in new ones.

Over the years, I’ve learned that keeping clients isn’t only about delivering good results. It’s also about trust. Clients need to know they can rely on you, especially when something goes wrong. And once that trust is broken, it’s very hard to win back. Alpha Market Flow reports that 72% of repeat buyers say they would permanently abandon a brand after a single trust-breaking incident. That’s why I try to communicate openly, address problems early and never make promises I can’t keep.

Business impact: Focusing on existing clients gives my business more predictable revenue and reduces the constant pressure to find newly introduced projects.

One small habit that has made a major difference in my marketing work is paying attention to how customers describe their problems. I’ve learned that people rarely use the same language as the companies selling to them.

I applied this approach with an invoicing software client by studying support tickets, sales calls, live chats, reviews and internal website searches. Customers weren’t asking for an “accounts receivable automation platform.” They wanted to stop chasing late payments, avoid invoice mistakes and save time creating invoices.

I used those insights to build the brand’s narrative. On the client’s own website, I rewrote key pages around the problems customers actually described and added public pricing and customer case studies. Through digital PR campaigns, I made sure that whenever the brand was mentioned on other websites, the surrounding text explained a specific customer problem and how the software solved it. Instead of simply getting mentions, I was consistently telling the same story: This is the tool that helps you get paid on time.

It has been revealed that over six months, the brand earned more than 60 mentions across industry publications, comparison articles and digital PR coverage. Organic traffic increased by 25%, while organic demo requests grew by 44%.

I started using this approach long before AI search became popular, but I believe it’s even more important today. After analyzing 2 million AI citations, Discovered Labs found that content closely matching consumers’ questions was more likely to be cited, with stronger alignment associated with roughly 30% more citations. This reinforces something I’ve believed for years: The more consistently you connect your brand to the problems it solves, the easier it becomes for people, and now AI tools, to understand what your business offers.

Recent findings suggest that business impact: Listening to how customers describe their problems now shapes how I approach every client. When a brand is consistently connected to the problems its customers want solved, it becomes easier to find, easier to trust and easier for both people and AI tools to recommend.

One habit that has made a real difference in my business is building relationships with journalists before I have something to pitch. I’ve learned that the best media relationships develop gradually, through genuine conversations rather than requests for coverage.

Sources indicate that I look for opportunities to connect with journalists at conferences, industry events and in private communities we’re both part of. I also try to understand what matters to them and how I might be helpful, especially when they’re looking for information, sources or expert opinions. I don’t approach every interaction with the expectation of getting something in return.

Even when I’m reading for pleasure or watching television, I often notice journalists whose work interests me. I’ll make a note of their names, look into what they cover and find a natural opportunity to introduce myself. Over time, these small interactions can turn into genuine professional relationships.

Industry observers note that I’ve learned that it’s far better to send a relevant story to 10 or 15 journalists I’ve built relationships with than to blast the same email to 1,500 strangers. Relationships don’t guarantee coverage, but they give you something a mass email can’t: an existing conversation and a better understanding of what each journalist finds interesting.

According to recent reports, these relationships matter to journalists, too. According to CoinFunnel, 53% of journalists consider their relationships with PR professionals important or very important to their success. That reinforces something I’ve learned through experience: Effective PR begins long before you have a story to pitch.

In a recent development, business impact: Instead of starting from zero every time I have a story to share, I already know which journalists are likely to care about it. That saves time, leads to better conversations and makes it far more likely that my ideas, and my clients’ stories, actually get published.

It has been revealed that if you want to try this yourself, you don’t necessarily have to build these habits one at a time. Many experts recommend starting with a single habit, and that’s good advice in most cases. But because these habits cover very different parts of life and work, I think it’s fine to start a few of them at once.

Taking a daily walk won’t get in the way of nurturing relationships with journalists, and working with a trainer won’t stop you from spending more time with existing clients. Pick the ones that fit your life and your business, give them a few months, and pay attention to what changes. Small habits rarely feel key in the moment, but over time, they can shape the kind of business you build.

When people talk about growing a business, they usually focus on the big moves: landing a major client, launching a newly introduced service or hiring the right team. But when I look back at my own journey, some of the things that helped me most were much smaller and easier to overlook.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote, “The first wealth is health.” I didn’t fully appreciate that until I saw how much my energy, focus and decisions depended on how well I took care of myself. Over time, together, they made a real difference. Here are the little habits that I personally believe helped my business the most.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am.

Recent findings suggest that sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, declared a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the firm plans to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

It has been revealed that panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

Sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, stated Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

Industry observers note that “This is a really crucial blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he said. “We have to take new technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”.

While the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky remarked. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

Recent findings suggest that batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

Recent findings suggest that berdichevsky mentioned Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

Sources indicate that in August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The firm must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

The startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

The tech giant has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round revealed in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

Recent findings suggest that seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

Group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently announced plans for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky said.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our tech giant’s history,” he said.

According to recent reports, the first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

Sources indicate that “None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky mentioned. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”.

In a recent development, asset manager Bitwise has filed an S-1 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission for a spot Zcash (ZEC) exchange-traded fund. The document appeared in the SEC's database on Nov. 17, 2026. On Wednesday, ZEC rose to $975 before it pulled back to around $927.

Zcash is often called a "more secret" version of Bitcoin. According to the S-1, the Zcash network supports two types of transactions, and the "shielded" ones use a form of zero-knowledge cryptography known as zk-SNARKs. Holders of shielded Zcash "may selectively disclose transaction information to third parties," the filing says.

Bitwise's fund will not use this feature. "The Trust does not engage in shielded transactions in connection with its activities," according to the document.

Industry observers note that the shares are expected to list on the Dallas-based Texas Stock Exchange (TXSE) under the ticker ZEC. According to the S-1, Coinbase Custody Trust Tech giant will act as the Zcash custodian, and BNY Mellon will serve as the cash custodian. Bitwise also wrote that "the Trust will not stake or otherwise seek to derive additional Zcash from its holdings." The sponsor fee in the filing is listed as "0.___% per annum.".

In the risk section of the S-1, Bitwise wrote that "a number of digital asset trading platforms have delisted Zcash, restricted trading in Zcash or declined to support Zcash." According to the filing, many of these platforms cited regulatory or compliance concerns.

The platforms that still support Zcash "do so only with respect to transparent addresses and do not permit deposits or withdrawals to or from shielded addresses," the document says. Bitwise also pointed to new EU rules that take effect on July 10, 2027. According to the S-1, the rules will "prohibit credit institutions, financial institutions and crypto-asset service providers in the European Union" from keeping accounts in such assets.

Bitwise CIO Matt Hougan named Zcash one of his top three assets for the decade in September, alongside Bitcoin and tokenization projects. Three days before the S-1 filing, he called ZEC a "golden mean" between open Bitcoin and anonymous Monero in an interview.

It has been revealed that grayscale's Zcash fund (ZCSH) has traded on NYSE Arca since August 2026, and the Winklevoss brothers filed for their own Zcash ETF on Nasdaq in October. ZCSH held $496.79 million as of the Nov. 17 close, according to SoSoValue. The fund has attracted $168.76 million in net inflows since its launch, and it recorded no inflows on Nov. 17, when Bitwise filed its S-1.
